questions.explanation: A repair that only maintains an asset at its original estimate is revenue expenditure, charged as a running cost of the period. It would be capital expenditure only if it improved the generator or extended its useful life or capacity. Receipts are money coming in, so neither receipt option fits a repair payment.

questions.question: A firm in Surulere buys a plot of land on which to build a new warehouse. This purchase is
questions.explanation: Buying land for use in the business acquires a non-current asset, so it is capital expenditure. Revenue and recurrent expenditure are the same idea, the day-to-day running costs, so neither fits a one-off purchase of land. A revenue receipt is income such as sales.

questions.question: A UNILAG department spends money to increase the capacity of its printing machine so that it can print twice as many pages per hour. This spending is

options.a: Revenue expenditure, because the machine is used every day
options.b: Revenue expenditure, because it keeps the machine at its original estimate
options.c: A capital receipt, because the machine becomes more valuable
options.d: Capital expenditure, because it increases the capacity of a non-current asset

questions.explanation: Increasing the capacity of a non-current asset is capital expenditure, because the asset ends up better than it was. Revenue expenditure would apply only to running costs or to repairs that keep the machine at its original estimate, which is not the case here. A capital receipt is money received, not spent.

questions.question: A furniture maker in Ikorodu records several inflows of money during the month. Which of them is a capital receipt?

options.a: Cash received from the sale of goods
options.b: A loan received from a bank in Lagos
options.c: Money received from customers for services rendered
options.d: Daily takings from its furniture showroom

questions.explanation: Capital receipts are owner capital, loans and the proceeds from selling non-current assets, so a bank loan is a capital receipt. Cash from selling goods, fees for services and daily shop takings are all sales or operating income, which makes them revenue receipts.

questions.question: A trader in Balogun market sells an old delivery van that the business no longer needs. The cash received from the sale is
questions.explanation: Proceeds from selling a non-current asset are a capital receipt. It is tempting to call it a revenue receipt because cash comes in, but revenue receipts are sales of trading goods and other operating income, and the van was never trading stock. The two expenditure options describe money going out.

questions.question: The owner of a provisions shop in Mushin pays N500,000 of personal savings into the business as additional capital. For the business, this is
questions.explanation: Money introduced by the owner as capital is a capital receipt. It is not a revenue receipt or operating income, because it does not come from selling goods or from the business's normal operations. Revenue expenditure is a running cost paid out, not money received.

questions.question: Money flowing into a business can be a capital receipt or a revenue receipt. Which of these inflows is a revenue receipt?

options.a: Proceeds from selling an old generator
options.c: Additional capital brought in by the owner
options.d: A loan from a microfinance bank

questions.explanation: Revenue receipts are sales and other operating income, so money from selling goods to customers is a revenue receipt. A loan, the proceeds from selling a non-current asset such as a generator, and capital brought in by the owner are all capital receipts.

questions.question: Owner capital, loans and asset sale proceeds are typical capital receipts. Which item below does NOT belong in that category?

options.b: Proceeds from selling office furniture no longer needed
options.d: A long-term loan from a bank

questions.explanation: Cash sales of trading goods are a revenue receipt, because sales are part of operating income. Loans, proceeds from selling non-current assets such as unwanted furniture, and capital introduced by the owner are the three kinds of capital receipt.

questions.question: A business wants to list its capital receipts for the year. Which group contains capital receipts and nothing else?

options.a: Cash sales, credit sales, proceeds from selling non-current assets
options.b: Loans received, cash sales, other operating income
options.c: Owner's capital, loans received, cash sales
options.d: Owner's capital, loans received, proceeds from selling non-current assets

questions.explanation: Capital receipts are exactly these three: owner capital, loans, and proceeds from selling non-current assets. Each of the other groups slips in sales or operating income, which are revenue receipts, so none of them is made up of capital receipts only.

questions.question: Which pair correctly shows a capital receipt followed by a revenue receipt?

options.a: Bank loan received; sales of goods
options.b: Sales of goods; other operating income
options.c: Proceeds from sale of old machine; owner's additional capital
options.d: Sales of goods; bank loan received

questions.explanation: A bank loan is a capital receipt and sales of goods are a revenue receipt, so this pair is in the right order. Putting sales first reverses the order. The pair of old machine proceeds and owner's capital is two capital receipts, while sales and operating income are two revenue receipts.

questions.question: Which of the following is a revenue expenditure for a supermarket in Lekki?

options.b: Purchase of new shelving for the shop
options.c: Installation of a new cold room

questions.explanation: Salaries are part of the day-to-day cost of running the business, so they are revenue (recurrent) expenditure. Shelving, a cold room and a delivery van are all non-current assets bought for long-term use, which makes them capital expenditure.

questions.question: Which statement best explains the difference between capital expenditure and revenue expenditure?

options.a: Capital expenditure covers the day-to-day running costs, while revenue expenditure buys non-current assets
options.b: Capital expenditure buys or improves non-current assets, while revenue expenditure covers the day-to-day running costs
options.c: Capital expenditure is money received from owners, while revenue expenditure is money received from customers
options.d: Capital expenditure is paid in cash, while revenue expenditure is paid by cheque

questions.explanation: The distinction rests on what the spending is for: capital expenditure buys, improves or extends non-current assets, while revenue expenditure meets the ordinary running costs of the business. The reversed statement swaps the two definitions. The method of payment, cash or cheque, has nothing to do with the classification.

questions.question: When part of the cost of a machine is charged to the income statement each year as depreciation, which accounting concept is being applied?
questions.explanation: Depreciation charges the expired portion of capital expenditure as an expense, so that the cost of the machine is matched against the revenue it helps to earn each year. The business entity concept is about separating the business from its owner, and money measurement only says items must be measurable in money, so neither explains spreading the cost.

questions.question: The expired portion of capital expenditure that is charged as an expense each period is known as
questions.explanation: Depreciation is the part of a non-current asset's cost that has been used up and is charged as an expense of the period. A prepayment is an expense paid in advance and an accrued expense is one incurred but not yet paid; neither relates to using up a non-current asset. Drawings are amounts the owner takes out for private use.

questions.question: A Lagos transport company spends money on its bus engine, which extends the bus's useful life by 30 months. In the ledger, the cost is best

options.a: Charged to the income statement as a repair expense
options.b: Added to the cost of the bus in the non-current asset account
options.c: Credited to the bus account as a reduction in its cost
options.d: Treated as drawings by the owner

questions.explanation: Because the work extends the bus's useful life, it is capital expenditure and is added to the cost of the asset. Charging it to the income statement would treat it as an ordinary repair, which is right only for repairs that keep the asset at its original estimate. Crediting the bus account would reduce the asset, and drawings are for the owner's private use.

questions.question: A firm in Ikeja pays to repair a machine so that it keeps working at its original estimate. Where should the cost be charged?

options.a: To the income statement as an expense of the period
options.b: To the machine account as part of its cost
options.c: To the statement of financial position as a non-current asset
options.d: To the owner's capital account as drawings

questions.explanation: A repair that only maintains the machine at its original estimate is revenue expenditure, so it is charged to the income statement for the period. Adding it to the machine account or showing it as a non-current asset would treat it as capital expenditure, which is only correct when the asset is improved or its life is extended.

questions.question: A firm in Ikeja spends the following: new machine N800,000; transport of the new machine N20,000; installation of the new machine N30,000; repair of an old machine to keep it at its original estimate N15,000; staff salaries N100,000. What is the total capital expenditure?
questions.explanation: Capital expenditure includes the full cost of getting the new machine ready for use: 800,000 + 20,000 + 30,000 = N850,000. Taking only the N800,000 price leaves out transport and installation, which are part of the asset's cost. N865,000 wrongly adds the maintenance repair, which is revenue expenditure, and N965,000 also adds the salaries.

questions.question: During the month, a business received: cash sales N900,000; a bank loan N500,000; proceeds from selling an old van N300,000; additional capital from the owner N400,000. What is the total of capital receipts?
questions.explanation: Capital receipts are the loan, the van proceeds and the owner's capital: 500,000 + 300,000 + 400,000 = N1,200,000. N2,100,000 wrongly includes the cash sales, which are a revenue receipt. N800,000 forgets the owner's capital, and N900,000 is just the sales figure.

questions.question: A business pays: salaries N150,000; repairs to keep equipment at its original estimate N40,000; a new delivery vehicle N2,000,000; installation of automatic controls in the vehicle N120,000; electricity N25,000. What is the total revenue expenditure?
questions.explanation: Revenue expenditure is the day-to-day running cost: salaries, maintenance repairs and electricity, 150,000 + 40,000 + 25,000 = N215,000. N335,000 wrongly includes the automatic controls, which improve the vehicle and are capital expenditure. N175,000 leaves out the maintenance repairs, and N2,120,000 is the capital expenditure total.

questions.question: A haulage firm in Kano made four payments this month. Which one should NOT be treated as capital expenditure?

options.a: Installing automatic controls in a vehicle
options.b: Buying a new generator for the factory
options.c: Paying for routine repairs that keep a vehicle at its original estimate
options.d: Overhauling an engine so that it lasts 30 months longer

questions.explanation: Routine repairs that only maintain an asset at its original estimate are revenue expenditure. Buying a generator acquires a non-current asset, installing automatic controls improves one, and an overhaul that adds 30 months extends its life, so all three are capital expenditure.

questions.question: Money received from the owner as capital, from loans, and from selling non-current assets is collectively known as
questions.explanation: These three inflows are the capital receipts of a business. Revenue receipts and operating income are the sales and other income earned from normal trading, which these are not. Capital expenditure is money spent on non-current assets, not money received.

questions.question: Sales and other operating income of a business are classified as
questions.explanation: Revenue receipts are the sales and other income earned from the business's normal operations. Capital receipts are owner capital, loans and proceeds from selling non-current assets. The two expenditure options are money spent, not money earned.

questions.question: Which of the following is a necessary condition for a change in accounting method overriding the consistency concept?

options.a: The effects of such change on reported profits should not be communicated
options.b: The users of the financial statement should be informed of the change
options.c: The changes should be made for the purpose of profit manipulation
options.d: The changes should be made frequently

questions.explanation: A business may change an accounting method only when the change gives a fairer view, and users of the financial statements must be told about the change and its effect. Option A is the opposite of what is required, while options C and D describe profit manipulation and frequent changes, which are exactly what the consistency concept is meant to prevent.

questions.question: Depreciation follows which accounting concept
questions.explanation: Depreciation spreads the cost of a non-current asset over the periods that benefit from using it, so each period's revenue carries a fair share of that cost - this is the matching concept. Option A is tempting because depreciation starts from the asset's cost, but the reason it is charged every year is to match cost against the revenue it helps to earn.

questions.question: Which of the following accounting concepts is violated by the inclusion of private assets in the balance sheet of a business by its owner?
questions.explanation: The entity concept treats the business as separate from its owner, so the owner's private assets must not appear in the business balance sheet. Option B, materiality, is about whether an item is big enough to matter, and option D, consistency, is about using the same methods each year - neither is broken here.

questions.question: Which of the following is an implication of the entity concept to a sole trader?

options.a: Liability of the owner is limited
options.b: Private use of business assets increases owners capital
options.c: Business can sue and be sued separately
options.d: Private use of business assets reduces owners capital

questions.explanation: Under the entity concept the business is separate from the owner, so when the owner uses business assets privately it is treated as drawings, which reduces the owner's capital. Option B gets the direction wrong, and options A and C describe features of a limited company, not a sole trader.

questions.question: Accountants might recognize losses but not gains in certain situations. For example, the company might write-down the cost of inventory, but will not write-up the cost of inventory. Which principle/guideline is associated with this action?
questions.explanation: Conservatism (prudence) says losses should be recognised as soon as they are expected but gains only when they are realised, which is why inventory is written down but never written up above cost. Materiality (Option B) is about whether an amount is big enough to matter, and the monetary unit idea (Option A) is about measuring in money.

questions.question: Which principle/guideline requires the company's financial statements to have footnotes containing information that is important to users of the financial statements?
questions.explanation: The full disclosure principle requires financial statements to include all information that would matter to users, often given in notes (footnotes) to the accounts. The economic entity idea (Option B) keeps business and owner separate, and conservatism (Option C) is about being cautious with gains and losses.

questions.question: Which principle/guideline justifies a company violating an accounting principle because the amounts are immaterial?
questions.explanation: The materiality concept allows a business to ignore strict accounting treatment for amounts that are too small to influence users' decisions. Conservatism (Option A) is about caution with gains and losses, full disclosure (Option B) asks for more information rather than less, and reconciliation (Option C) is not an accounting principle.

questions.question: The creative chief executive of a corporation who is personally responsible for numerous inventions and innovations is not reported as an asset on the corporation's balance sheet. The accounting principle/guideline that prevents the corporation for reporting this person as an asset is
questions.explanation: Under the cost principle, items are recorded at the amount actually paid in a transaction; the business never paid a measurable price to acquire the chief executive's talent, so it cannot be shown as an asset. Conservatism (option A) is about caution with gains and losses, going concern (option C) assumes the business will continue, and matching (option D) links expenses to revenues.

questions.question: Which principle/guideline directs a company to show all the expenses related to its revenues of a specified period even if the expenses were not paid in that period?
questions.explanation: The matching principle requires expenses to be recorded in the same period as the revenues they helped earn, whether or not they have been paid. Going concern (Option D) assumes the business will continue, and the cost and monetary unit ideas (Options C and A) are about measurement.

questions.question: The personal assets of the owner of a company will not appear on the company's balance sheet because of which principle/guideline?
questions.explanation: The economic entity (business entity) concept treats the business as separate from its owner, so the owner's personal assets are not shown on the business's balance sheet. The cost principle (Option A) and monetary unit idea (Option C) concern how items are measured, not whose items they are.

questions.question: A very large corporation's financial statements have the dollar amounts rounded to the nearest $1,000. Which accounting principle/guideline justifies not reporting the amounts to the penny?
questions.explanation: Rounding to the nearest $1,000 is acceptable because such small differences would not affect the decisions of users of a very large company's statements - this is materiality. The monetary unit concept (Option A) only says items are measured in money, and full disclosure (Option C) is about including important information.

questions.question: A company borrowed $100,000 in December and will make its only payment for interest when the note comes due six months later. The total interest for the six months will be $3,600. On the December income statement the accountant reported Interest Expense of $600. This action was the result of which accounting principle/guideline?
questions.explanation: One month's interest ($3,600 / 6 = $600) relates to December, so it is recorded as December's expense even though it will be paid later - this is the matching principle. Revenue recognition (Option C) deals with when income is recorded, not expenses, and cost (Option A) concerns the amount recorded for assets.

questions.question: A company sold merchandise of $8,000 to a customer in December. The company's sales terms require the customer to pay the company in 30 days. The company's income statement reported the sale in December. This is proper under which accounting principle/guideline?
questions.explanation: Revenue recognition says revenue is recorded when it is earned, which here is when the goods were sold in December, not when cash is received. Matching (Option D) is about recording expenses in the same period as related revenues, and full disclosure (Option A) is about notes and information.

questions.question: When the accountant has to choose between two acceptable alternatives, the accountant should select the alternative that will report less profit, less asset amount, or a greater liability amount. This is based upon which principle/guideline?
questions.explanation: Conservatism (prudence) means that when two methods are acceptable, the accountant chooses the one that gives the lower profit or asset figure or the higher liability, to avoid overstating the business's position. Materiality (Option C) is about the size of an item, and cost (Option B) concerns recording items at what was paid.

questions.question: An asset with a cost of $120,000 is depreciated over its useful life of 10 years rather than expensing the entire amount when it is purchased. This complies with which principle/guideline?
questions.explanation: Depreciating the $120,000 asset over 10 years ($120,000 / 10 = $12,000 a year with no residual value) spreads its cost over the periods that benefit from using it, which is the matching principle. The cost principle (Option A) decides the $120,000 recorded, not how it is spread, and revenue recognition (Option B) concerns income.

questions.question: A corporation pays its annual property tax bill of approximately $12,000 in one payment each December 28. During the year, the corporation's monthly income statements report Property Tax Expense of $1,000. This is an example of which accounting principle/guideline?
questions.explanation: Charging $12,000 / 12 = $1,000 of property tax to each month spreads the expense over the periods it relates to, even though it is paid once a year - that is matching. Conservatism (Option A) is about caution, and going concern (Option D) assumes the business will continue.

questions.question: A large company purchases a $250 digital camera and expenses it immediately instead of recording it as an asset and depreciating it over its useful life. This practice may be acceptable because of which principle/guideline?
questions.explanation: A $250 camera is so small compared with a large company's totals that expensing it immediately will not mislead anyone, so materiality allows it. Option B, matching, would actually require the camera to be capitalised and depreciated over its useful life. Conservatism (Option D) is about caution with gains and losses rather than ignoring small amounts.

questions.question: A retailer wishes to report its merchandise inventory on its balance sheet at its retail value. This would violate which accounting principle/guideline?
questions.explanation: The cost principle says inventory and other assets are recorded at what the business paid, not at their selling (retail) price, so reporting inventory at retail value breaks it. Full disclosure (Option B) is about notes and information, and materiality (Option D) is about the size of items.

questions.question: Near the end of the current year, a company required a customer to pay $200,000 as a deposit for work that is to begin in the following year. At the end of the current year the company reported the $200,000 as a liability on its balance sheet. Which accounting principle/guideline prevented the company from reporting the $200,000 on its income statement for the current year?
questions.explanation: Revenue recognition says income is recorded only when it is earned; the work starts next year, so the $200,000 deposit is unearned and shown as a liability. Going concern (Option A) assumes the business will continue, and full disclosure (Option D) concerns notes, not when revenue is recorded.

questions.question: Which principle/guideline is associated with the assumption that the company will continue on long enough to carry out its objectives and commitments?
questions.explanation: The going concern concept assumes the business will continue operating long enough to carry out its objectives and commitments, which is why assets are carried at cost rather than at what they would fetch if sold off. The time period idea (Option C) divides the business life into periods, and economic entity (Option A) separates business from owner.

questions.question: Accrual accounting is based on this principle/guideline.
questions.explanation: Accrual accounting records expenses in the period they help earn revenue, whether or not cash has changed hands - this is the matching principle. Cost (Option A) and monetary unit (Option D) are about measurement, and full disclosure (Option B) is about giving enough information.

questions.question: Which principle/guideline allows a company to ignore the change in the purchasing power of the dollar over time?
questions.explanation: The monetary unit concept assumes money keeps a stable value, so accounts are kept in money terms without adjusting for changes in purchasing power (inflation). Cost (Option A) records items at what was paid, and economic entity (Option B) separates the business from its owner.

questions.question: Public utilities' balance sheets list the plant assets before the current assets. This is acceptable under which accounting principle/guideline?
questions.explanation: Industry practices allow an industry to depart from the usual presentation when its special nature makes another approach more useful, as with public utilities listing plant assets first. Materiality (Option C) is about small amounts, and conservatism (Option A) is about caution, so neither explains this presentation.

questions.question: Which principle/guideline requires a company's balance sheet to report its land at the amount the company paid to acquire the land, even if the land could be sold today at a significantly higher amount?
questions.explanation: Under the cost (historical cost) principle, assets such as land are recorded at the amount paid to acquire them, even if their market value later rises. The monetary unit idea (Option C) says items are measured in money, and full disclosure (Option D) concerns giving extra information in notes.

questions.question: Large corporations should report revenues on their income statements when the
questions.explanation: Under accrual accounting and the revenue recognition principle, revenue is reported when it is earned, for example when goods are delivered or services performed. Option A, when cash is received, describes cash basis accounting, which large corporations do not use for their income statements.

questions.question: Consistency concept does not imply one of the following.

options.a: Possibility of comparing financial statements over time
options.b: Treatment of like items in a similar manner
options.c: All companies in the same industry should use the same methods
options.d: Effect of changes in the adopted method is properly disclosed

questions.explanation: The consistency concept means the same business should treat similar items the same way from year to year, so its statements can be compared over time, and any change in method must be disclosed. It does not require different companies in the same industry to use the same methods, which is why Option C is the exception. Options A, B and D are all part of what consistency means.

questions.question: The basic points of agreement on which financial accounting theory and practice is founded is termed
questions.explanation: Accounting concepts are the basic assumptions or points of agreement - such as going concern, accruals and consistency - on which accounting theory and practice are built. Option B, accounting theory, is the body of reasoning that is built on those concepts rather than the basic points themselves.

questions.question: One of the following is not a limitation of Accounting

options.b: It is not free from bias.
options.c: It ignores changes in price levels.
options.d: It provides a permanent record of business transactions.

questions.explanation: Keeping a permanent, organised record of transactions is one of the main benefits of accounting, so it is not a limitation. Option C is a real limitation, because figures are kept at historical cost and do not reflect inflation, just as options A and B are: accounting shows only quantitative information and leaves room for bias in estimates and judgements.

questions.question: The rule to recognise revenue when it is reasonably certain and recognise expenses as soon as they are reasonably possible is known as
questions.explanation: Conservatism (prudence) says revenue and profits are recognised only when reasonably certain, while expenses and losses are provided for as soon as they are reasonably possible. Option C, realisation, only deals with when revenue is earned and says nothing about recognising expenses early. Matching (Option B) links expenses to the revenue of the same period.

questions.question: In order that financial statements report financial performance fairly and consistently, they are prepared according to widely accepted accounting standards. These standards are referred to as
questions.explanation: The widely accepted body of rules for preparing financial statements is called Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP). Options B, C and D are near misses: the term uses "Accepted" not "Acceptable", and "Principles" in the plural.

questions.question: A trader in Balogun market bought 80 bags of rice for N2,400,000 and sold 60 of them during the period. Applying the matching concept, what is the cost of sales for the period?
questions.explanation: Matching charges only the cost of the goods actually sold against the revenue they earned: 60/80 x 2,400,000 = N1,800,000. N600,000 is the cost of the 20 unsold bags, which is carried forward as inventory, not charged. Charging the full N2,400,000 ignores matching altogether.

questions.question: A firm in Ikeja buys a generator for N750,000, pays N15,000 to transport it and N10,000 to install it. Under the accounting cost concept, at what amount should the generator be recorded?
questions.explanation: Under the accounting cost concept, the cost of an asset includes its purchase price plus transport and installation: 750,000 + 15,000 + 10,000 = N775,000. Recording only the N750,000 price leaves out costs needed to get the generator working. N765,000 and N760,000 each leave out one of the two extra costs.

questions.question: A firm in Ikeja receives a customer's order in March, delivers the goods and invoices the customer in April, and is paid in May. Under the realisation concept, in which month is the revenue realised?

options.b: June, when the accounts are prepared

questions.explanation: Revenue is realised when the goods are sold and the customer incurs a liability to pay, which happens on delivery in April. Receiving an order in March creates no legal right to receive money, so it is not realisation. Waiting for the cash in May would confuse realisation with cash receipt.

questions.question: A company accounts for an asset it holds under a lease in line with the economic reality of the arrangement rather than its legal form. Which concept is being applied?
questions.explanation: Substance over form requires transactions to be accounted for by their economic substance rather than their legal form, and leases are the usual example. Historical cost is about recording assets at what they cost, and objectivity is about evidence free from bias; neither deals with substance versus legal form.

questions.question: The accounting concept that extends objectivity so that financial reports do not favour any particular group of users is
questions.explanation: Fairness is described as an extension of objectivity: reports should be prepared so that they favour no group. Consistency is about using the same methods from period to period, materiality is about disclosing significant items, and periodicity is about reporting at regular intervals.

questions.question: Limited companies prepare and publish their financial statements every year so that performance can be reviewed at regular intervals. This reflects which concept?
questions.explanation: The periodicity concept says performance is reviewed periodically, and limited companies report annually. Going concern is the assumption that the business will continue operating, which is different from reporting at regular intervals. Consistency concerns using the same methods each period, not how often reports are made.

questions.question: A manufacturing company in Ota is facing a large lawsuit that could cost it heavily. It reports this in its financial statements even though the information is unfavourable. Which convention is it following?
questions.explanation: Full disclosure requires all significant information to be disclosed, even when it is unfavourable to the business. Materiality decides whether an item is significant enough to show separately, but it is full disclosure that insists on reporting bad news. Consistency is about keeping the same methods, and money measurement is about recording only items measurable in money.

questions.question: Financial accounting has several weaknesses. Identify the one that is a recognised limitation.

options.a: It records every transaction on a double-entry basis
options.b: It reports on the business as a whole, not by product, process or department
options.c: It provides evidence that makes an audit possible
options.d: It summarises the results of the business for a period

questions.explanation: Financial accounting reports only on the whole concern, so it does not show how individual products, processes or departments are performing, which is a recognised limitation. Providing audit evidence, recording transactions by double entry and summarising results for a period are useful features of accounting, not limitations.

questions.question: A company in Lagos still reports a building bought many years ago at its original cost, even though inflation has greatly changed the value of the naira since then. This illustrates which limitation of financial accounting?

options.a: It does not give the cost of products manufactured
options.c: It is too technical for non-accountants
options.d: It cannot compare actual results with budget

questions.explanation: Financial accounting records items at historical cost and ignores changes in the price level, so the building's figure no longer reflects current values after years of inflation. Being too technical, not comparing results with budget, and not costing products are also limitations, but they have nothing to do with inflation and old asset values.

questions.question: When the owner invests money in a business, it is recorded as capital, treated as an amount the business owes to the owner. Which concept explains this treatment?
questions.explanation: The business entity concept treats the business as separate from its owner, so the owner's investment is recorded as capital, a liability of the business towards the owner. Dual aspect explains why the investment is recorded twice, but not why the owner is treated as a separate party. Money measurement and going concern do not deal with the owner's relationship to the business.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four accounting conventions?
questions.explanation: The four accounting conventions are conservatism, consistency, full disclosure and materiality. Going concern is an accounting concept, not one of these conventions: it assumes the business will continue operating in the foreseeable future.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: From which of the following are entries posted into the ledger?
questions.explanation: Subsidiary books (the books of prime entry, such as the day books and journal) are where transactions are first recorded, and their entries are then posted into the ledger. Options A, B and D are statements prepared at the end of a period from ledger balances, so they come after the ledger, not before it.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: In which of the following book of prime entry would purchase of equipment on credit be captured?
questions.explanation: The purchases journal records only credit purchases of goods meant for resale, so buying equipment on credit, which is a non-current asset, goes into the journal proper. Option B is the tempting trap, and option A is wrong because no cash moved at the time of purchase.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: Recording of transactions must be done on double entry basis in which of the following subsidiary books?
questions.explanation: The cash book is both a book of prime entry and part of the ledger, so the cash and bank accounts kept in it form one side of the double entry directly. Option A, the journal proper, shows both sides of an entry, but it is still only a book of prime entry and its items must be posted to the ledger. Options B and C are also books of prime entry only.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: The book of original entry is the definition of a
questions.explanation: A journal is the book of original (prime) entry where transactions are first recorded before they are posted. The ledger (Option B) is where the entries are posted afterwards, so it is the book of final entry rather than original entry.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: A note informing credit suppliers of charges to their accounts for goods returned is called
questions.explanation: A debit note is sent by a buyer to a supplier to show that the supplier's account in the buyer's books has been debited, for example for goods returned. Option C, a purchases returns note, is not the standard name for this document. Option A is a written promise to pay money, and Option B is a document used on the selling side.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: Which document is used for undercharge of commodities
questions.explanation: If a seller has undercharged a customer, it sends a debit note to increase the amount the customer owes. Option A, a credit note, is used for the opposite case, an overcharge or goods returned. A proforma invoice (D) is a quotation-style invoice sent before a sale.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: ___ is used for overcharge
questions.explanation: When a customer has been overcharged, the seller sends a credit note to reduce the amount the customer owes. A debit note (B) is used to correct an undercharge. An invoice (D) records the original sale, and a proforma invoice (C) is sent before the sale is made.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: Which of the following documents should accompany a return of goods to a supplier?
questions.explanation: A debit note is sent to a supplier along with returned goods, telling the supplier that their account in the buyer's books is being reduced (debited) by the value of the return. Option D, a credit note, is the document the supplier sends back to confirm the reduction. Option B, a remittance advice, goes with a payment, and option C, a purchase invoice, is received when goods are bought.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: Which of the following are books of prime entry? 1 Sales day book; 2 Cash book; 3 Journal; 4 Purchase ledger
questions.explanation: Books of prime entry are where transactions are first recorded before posting to the ledger: the sales day book, the cash book and the journal all qualify. The purchase ledger is a ledger, not a book of prime entry, so option D is wrong. Options A and C leave out books that are genuinely books of prime entry.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: In which book of prime entry will a business record debit notes in respect of goods which have been sent back to suppliers?
questions.explanation: Goods sent back to suppliers are purchase returns (returns outwards), so the debit notes are recorded in the purchase returns day book. Option A (sales returns day book) is for goods returned by customers, and option D (purchase day book) records credit purchases, not returns. Option B is wrong because no cash changes hands on a return.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: Which of the following would be recorded in the sales daybook?
questions.explanation: The sales day book records credit sales, and its entries come from the sales invoices sent to customers. Option A (discounts allowed) is recorded in the cash book, and option C (credit notes received) would go in the purchase returns day book. Option D is wrong because trade discounts are deducted on the invoice and are not recorded in the books at all.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: In which of the following financial records or documents will trade discount be recorded?
questions.explanation: Trade discount is a reduction in list price shown only on the invoice; it is never entered in the books of account. That is why options A, B and C (cash book, purchases day book and general ledger) are wrong: they record only the net amount after the trade discount has already been taken off.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: The total value in the sales day book would be transferred to
questions.explanation: The sales day book lists credit sales, and its periodic total is posted to the credit side of the sales account, with each customer's account being debited. Option B is wrong because payables relate to suppliers, not sales, and option C has nothing to do with sales. Option D is ruled out because A is correct.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: Furniture and fittings purchased on credit (for resale) will first be recorded in the
questions.explanation: Because the furniture is bought for resale, it is stock in trade for this business, so a credit purchase of it is first recorded in the purchases journal. Option A, the journal proper, would be right only if the furniture were bought for use in the business as a non-current asset. Option D is wrong because no cash is paid on a credit purchase.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: The original evidence of a transaction, without which nothing should be recorded in the books, is called a
questions.explanation: Source documents, also called accounting documents, are the original evidence of every transaction, and nothing is recorded without one. A book of prime entry is where the transaction is first written up from that document, and the ledger and trial balance come even later in the process.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a function of source documents?

options.a: They provide evidence that makes an audit possible
options.b: They provide evidence that guards against fraud
options.c: They are signed by the parties, so they cannot easily be denied
options.d: They show the net profit or loss for the period

questions.explanation: Source documents serve as evidence: they guard against fraud, make audit possible, cannot easily be denied because the parties sign them, and are hard to alter. Showing net profit or loss is the job of the income statement, prepared at the end of the period, not of individual source documents.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: A purchase invoice received from a supplier is the source document for entries in the
questions.explanation: A purchase invoice is the original of the supplier's sales invoice, and it is used to write up the purchases day book for credit purchases. The sales day book is written up from the duplicate sales invoices the business issues, and the returns inwards book from credit notes issued to customers.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: A firm in Ikeja receives electricity on credit and later gets a document showing the amount it owes. This document is best described as a
questions.explanation: Bills are used for services supplied on credit, such as electricity, water or telephone, while invoices are used for goods. A credit note reduces what a buyer owes, and a payment voucher authorises a payment, so neither describes a charge for electricity.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: A trader in Balogun market issues a credit note to a customer who returned some goods. In the trader's books, the credit note represents
questions.explanation: A credit note issued by a business means its customer has returned goods, so it records returns on sales, also called returns inwards. Returns outwards would apply if the trader had received a credit note from a supplier. It reduces sales rather than adding to them, and it has nothing to do with discount.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: A customer returns damaged goods to a wholesaler in Idumota, and the wholesaler replaces them with new goods of the same kind. Which statement is correct?

options.a: A debit note must be issued to increase the customer's debt
options.b: A new sales invoice must be issued for the replacement goods
options.c: No credit note is needed because the goods were replaced
options.d: A credit note must be issued for the value of the damaged goods

questions.explanation: A credit note is issued to reduce a buyer's debt, but when returned goods are simply replaced, the debt is unchanged, so no credit note is needed. Issuing a credit note here would wrongly reduce what the customer owes, and a new invoice would wrongly charge the customer twice.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: Which of the following is a reason for returning goods that would lead to a credit note being issued?

options.a: The goods delivered were of the wrong specification
options.b: The customer paid by cheque instead of cash
options.c: The customer bought in bulk and qualified for trade discount
options.d: The customer paid within the cash discount period

questions.explanation: Goods are returned when they are damaged before delivery or are of the wrong specification, and a credit note is then issued to reduce the buyer's debt. Prompt payment and bulk buying relate to discounts, not returns, and paying by cheque does not involve returning anything.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: A seller in Ikeja discovers that delivery charges were left out of an invoice already sent to a customer. Which document should the seller send to increase the amount the customer owes?
questions.explanation: A seller uses a debit note to increase the amount a debtor owes, for example after undercharging or for omitted charges such as delivery. A credit note does the opposite and reduces the debt. A receipt acknowledges money received, and a payment voucher authorises a payment.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: Which document is checked and authorised by a responsible officer before cash is paid out?
questions.explanation: A payment voucher is an authorising document checked by a responsible officer before cash is paid. A pay-in slip is evidence of money lodged into the bank, a store issue voucher updates the store ledger, and a cheque counterfoil is the record kept after a cheque has been written.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: The main source document for the debit side of the bank column of the cash book is the
questions.explanation: The bank pay-in slip is evidence of lodgements into the bank, and lodgements are receipts entered on the debit side of the bank column. The cheque counterfoil is the tempting choice, but it is evidence of payments by cheque, which go on the credit side.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: Evidence of a payment made by cheque is provided by the
questions.explanation: The cheque counterfoil, or stub, is kept by the business as evidence of each payment made by cheque. A pay-in slip is evidence of money paid into the bank, which is the opposite direction. Invoices and credit notes relate to sales, purchases and returns rather than payments.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: When a customer pays cash to a shop in Lekki and is given a receipt, which statement is correct?

options.a: The original goes to the payer and the seller keeps the duplicate
options.b: Both copies are kept by the seller
options.c: The original goes to the bank and the seller keeps the duplicate
options.d: The seller keeps the original and the payer gets the duplicate

questions.explanation: With a receipt, the original is handed to the payer as proof of payment and the duplicate is kept by the seller for its records. Reversing the copies is the usual slip. The bank plays no part in a cash receipt, and keeping both copies would leave the payer without evidence.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: Which source document is used to update the store ledger when goods are released from the store?
questions.explanation: A store issue voucher records goods issued from the store and is used to update the store ledger. A payment voucher authorises cash payments, a bank statement shows the bank's record of the account, and a debit note deals with returns or undercharges.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: Day books and journals are names used for the books where transactions are first written up. Which term is NOT another name for these books?
questions.explanation: Books of prime (original) entry are also called day books, journals or subsidiary books. The ledger is different: it is the principal book of account to which entries are posted from the books of prime entry.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: How often are transactions recorded in the books of prime entry first recorded and then posted to the ledger?

options.a: Recorded daily, then posted to the ledger periodically, such as weekly, fortnightly or monthly
options.b: Recorded and posted to the ledger only once a year
options.c: Recorded weekly, then posted to the ledger only when the trial balance is drawn up
options.d: Recorded monthly, then posted to the ledger daily

questions.explanation: Transactions are first written up in the books of prime entry each day, and the totals are posted to the ledger at regular intervals such as weekly, fortnightly or monthly. Recording monthly and posting daily reverses the order of frequency, and waiting a whole year would make the records useless for control.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the reasons for keeping books of prime entry?

options.a: To show the financial position of the business at the end of the period
options.b: To help prevent errors, as their totals can be reconciled with individual accounts
options.c: To keep transactions in chronological order
options.d: To group the totals of transactions in one place

questions.explanation: Books of prime entry group transaction totals, explain transactions, keep them in date order and help prevent errors. Showing the financial position at the end of the period is the purpose of the statement of financial position, not of the day books.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: The source document for entries in the returns inwards book is the

options.b: Credit note issued to the customer
options.d: Debit note received from a supplier

questions.explanation: The returns inwards book records goods returned by customers, and the document behind each entry is the credit note the business issues to the customer. A debit note relating to a supplier concerns goods the business itself sends back, which belongs to the returns outwards side.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: How are entries in the purchases day book posted to the ledger?

options.a: Each supplier is credited in the purchases ledger and the total is debited to the purchases account
options.b: Each supplier is debited in the purchases ledger and the total is credited to the purchases account
options.c: Each supplier is credited in the sales ledger and the total is debited to the sales account
options.d: Each supplier is debited in the general ledger and the total is credited to cash

questions.explanation: Credit purchases increase what the business owes its suppliers, so each supplier's account in the purchases ledger is credited and the day book total is debited to purchases. Debiting suppliers reverses the entry, and the sales ledger and sales account relate to customers, not suppliers.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: In the general journal, the narration written below each entry gives

options.a: The folio number of the trial balance
options.b: The balance on the account after posting
options.c: The purpose and authority for the entry
options.d: The total of the day book for the month

questions.explanation: Each journal entry records the date, the accounts debited and credited, and a narration that explains the purpose and authority of the entry, usually beginning with "Being". Account balances appear in the ledger, not in the narration, and day book totals have nothing to do with it.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT recorded in the general journal (journal proper)?

options.a: Purchase of a non-current asset on credit
options.c: Credit sales of goods to customers

questions.explanation: The general journal records items that are not credit sales or purchases, such as opening entries, transfers, credit purchases of non-current assets, adjustments and corrections. Credit sales of goods go into the sales day book instead.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: When a new business in Ikeja opens its books, its assets total N1,450,000 and its liabilities total N320,000. In the opening journal entry, what is the capital figure?
questions.explanation: In an opening entry, assets are debited, liabilities are credited, and capital is the balancing credit: 1,450,000 - 320,000 = N1,130,000. N1,770,000 wrongly adds the liabilities instead of deducting them. Capital is a credit, not a debit, and N1,450,000 ignores the liabilities completely.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: Adamu owes a business N400,000. By agreement, Chika, another customer, takes over the debt. What is the journal entry?
questions.explanation: Chika now owes the business, so Chika's account is debited, and Adamu no longer owes, so Adamu's account is credited. Reversing the names would make Adamu owe more. No new sale or cash payment has taken place, so neither sales nor cash is involved.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: A business sells one of its motor vehicles on credit to Jebeleje. Which journal entry records the sale?
questions.explanation: Jebeleje now owes the business, so his account is debited, and the vehicle leaves the business, so the motor vehicle account is credited. Crediting sales is the common mistake: a vehicle is a non-current asset, not trading stock. Cash is not involved because the sale is on credit.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: A credit sale to Bisi is posted in error to the account of Bimbo, another customer. In which book of prime entry should the correction first be recorded?
questions.explanation: The correction of errors is one of the uses of the general journal, so a credit sale posted to the wrong customer is corrected there. The sales day book records new credit sales, not corrections, and the returns inwards book is only for goods returned by customers.

questions.topic: Source documents and books of prime entry
questions.question: A UNILAG department pays N1,500 for a messenger's transport fare. In which book is this small payment most likely to be recorded?
questions.explanation: The petty cash book is the book of prime entry for small transactions such as transport fares. The general journal handles items like opening entries and corrections, the purchases day book records credit purchases of goods, and the sales returns book records goods returned by customers.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: The column of a ledger account used for reference purpose is
questions.explanation: The folio column is used for cross-referencing, showing the page or account number where the other side of the entry can be found. Option A, Particulars, describes the name of the other account involved, and option C simply holds the money value.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: Which one of the following is the best description of a salary account?
questions.explanation: Salary is an expense, and expense and income accounts are nominal accounts; since it does not belong to a person or a physical asset, it is impersonal. Options A and B describe real accounts, which are for assets like buildings, and option D wrongly calls it personal.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: An entry on the right-hand side of a ledger account is
questions.explanation: In a T-account the left-hand side is the debit side and the right-hand side is the credit side. Option B is the left side, and option D is the figure left after totalling both sides.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: Where are the personal accounts of customers to whom goods are sold on credit found?
questions.explanation: The sales ledger holds the personal accounts of credit customers (debtors). Option A, the sales journal, is the book of prime entry where credit sales are first listed, not where customer accounts are kept.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: The listing of accounts that are available for posting transactions is the ____ of accounts.
questions.explanation: A chart of accounts is the list of all account names (and often numbers) available for recording transactions. A trial balance (Option A) lists account balances at a date, and the journal (Option B) records the transactions themselves.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: Principally, ledger accounts can be classified into:

options.a: Debtors ledger account and creditors ledger account
options.b: Nominal ledger account and sales ledger account
options.c: Main ledger account and subsidiary ledger account
options.d: Impersonal ledger account and personal-ledger account

questions.explanation: Ledger accounts are broadly classified into personal accounts (people and firms, such as debtors and creditors) and impersonal accounts (real accounts for assets and nominal accounts for incomes and expenses). Option A lists only two kinds of personal account, and option B mixes one impersonal ledger with one personal ledger. Option C describes how ledgers are organised rather than how accounts are classified.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of impersonal real ledger account
questions.explanation: Real accounts are impersonal accounts for assets and property, so a Motor Vehicle account is a real account. Debtors (B) and creditors (D) are personal accounts because they relate to people or firms, while Salary (C) is a nominal account for an expense.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: The ledger is often described as the
questions.explanation: The ledger is the principal book of account, holding the permanent records of assets, liabilities, income, expenses and capital. The book of original entry, subsidiary book and book of prime entry are all names for the day books and journals where transactions are first recorded before being posted to the ledger.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the contents of the ledger?

options.a: Original evidence of transactions such as invoices and receipts
options.b: Daily records of credit sales only
options.c: Permanent records of assets, liabilities, income, expenses and capital
options.d: A list of balances prepared to check arithmetical accuracy

questions.explanation: The ledger holds the permanent records of every class of item: assets, liabilities, income, expenses and capital. Daily records of credit sales belong in the sales day book, invoices and receipts are source documents, and a list of balances is the trial balance extracted from the ledger.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: A bookkeeper in Ikeja lists the benefits of keeping a ledger. Which item on her list is wrong, because it describes something the ledger does NOT do?

options.a: It shows the movements in each account
options.b: It provides the information needed for the income statement and statement of financial position
options.c: It is the record from which the trial balance is extracted
options.d: It is where transactions are first recorded in date order before posting

questions.explanation: The ledger keeps permanent records, provides information for the financial statements, shows the origin of each transaction, shows movements in each account and is the basis for the trial balance. Recording transactions first in date order is the role of the books of prime entry, from which entries are later posted to the ledger.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: A trader in Balogun market wants to see how the balance on her rent account changed during the month. Which feature of the ledger makes this possible?

options.a: It is signed by the parties, so it cannot be denied
options.b: It shows the movements in each account
options.c: It authorises payments before cash is released
options.d: It groups the totals of transactions in one place

questions.explanation: One importance of the ledger is that it shows the movements in each account, so the trader can follow every increase and decrease in rent. Grouping totals in one place is a reason for keeping books of prime entry, being signed by the parties describes source documents, and authorising payments is the role of a payment voucher.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: The trial balance is extracted from the
questions.explanation: The trial balance is a list of the balances on the ledger accounts, so it is extracted from the ledger. The day books are books of prime entry whose totals are posted to the ledger first, and source documents are the original evidence behind those entries.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: In a T account, the left-hand side and the right-hand side are respectively the
questions.explanation: A T account has Dr (debit) on the left and Cr (credit) on the right. Reversing them is the usual slip. The sides are not named after assets and liabilities, because every account, whatever its type, has a debit and a credit side.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: Each side of a T account usually has which columns?
questions.explanation: Each side of a T account is set out with Date, Particulars and Amount columns, with a folio column for reference. Date, invoice number and customer are the columns of a sales day book, and separate debit and credit columns side by side belong to the journal layout.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: Accounts can be grouped into three types. These are
questions.explanation: The three types of account are real (tangible things), personal (persons, companies and partnerships) and nominal (gains and losses). Sales, purchases and general are types of ledger, not types of account, and capital and revenue describe kinds of expenditure.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: Accounts that record tangible things such as cash, cars and goods are called
questions.explanation: Real accounts record tangible things the business owns, such as cash, cars and goods. Personal accounts are for persons, companies or partnerships, and nominal accounts are for gains and losses such as rent and salaries.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: Personal accounts generally arise from
questions.explanation: Personal accounts are kept for persons, companies or partnerships, and they arise from credit transactions, when someone owes the business or is owed by it. A pure cash transaction leaves no amount owing, so it does not need a personal account. Adjustments and depreciation involve nominal and real accounts.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: Accounts that record gains and losses, such as rent, salaries and electricity, are called
questions.explanation: Nominal accounts record gains and losses, including expenses such as rent, salaries and electricity and items such as discounts. Real accounts are for tangible assets, and personal accounts are for people and organisations the business deals with on credit.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: The rent account of a shop in Surulere is classified as a
questions.explanation: Rent is an expense, and expenses are gains and losses recorded in nominal accounts. It is not a real account, because rent is not a tangible thing the business owns. It is not personal either, because it records an expense rather than the account of the landlord.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: A business in Ikeja keeps a separate account for its electricity costs. This account is best described as
questions.explanation: Electricity is an expense, so its account is nominal, and nominal accounts are impersonal because they do not relate to a person or organisation. A real account is also impersonal, but it records tangible assets such as vehicles, not expenses. An account cannot be both personal and nominal.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: Mr Bello buys goods on credit from a wholesaler in Idumota. In the wholesaler's books, Mr Bello's account is a
questions.explanation: Mr Bello is a person dealing with the business on credit, so his account is a personal account. Real and nominal accounts are the two kinds of impersonal account, recording tangible things and gains or losses respectively, so they do not fit an account kept for a customer.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: Okafor and Sons, a partnership, supplies goods on credit to a supermarket in Lekki. In the supermarket's books, the account of Okafor and Sons is a
questions.explanation: Personal accounts are kept for persons, companies and partnerships, so the account of a partnership supplying goods on credit is personal. The purchases account is the tempting choice, but it is a nominal account recording the cost of goods bought, not the amount owed to a particular supplier.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: The land account of a manufacturing company in Ota is a
questions.explanation: Land is a tangible asset owned by the business, so its account is a real account. Nominal accounts record gains and losses such as rent and wages, and personal accounts are kept for persons and organisations, so neither describes land.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: The discount received account is classified as a
questions.explanation: Discount received is a gain to the business, and gains and losses are recorded in nominal accounts, which include discounts. It is not a real account because it is not a tangible thing, and it is not personal because it is not the account of a supplier or customer.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: A trader in Balogun market gives some of her goods as a gift to a charity. On which side of the goods (real) account is this recorded?

options.a: Neither side, because no money changes hands
options.b: Both sides, as a contra entry

questions.explanation: Real accounts are debited with additions and credited with disposals, items damaged beyond use, or gifts given out. The goods leave the business, so the goods account is credited. Even though no money is received, the business has lost goods, so the transaction must still be recorded.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: A business buys a new delivery van. On which side of the motor vehicle (real) account is the purchase recorded?

options.b: Neither side, until the van is paid for
options.d: The side of the supplier's account only

questions.explanation: Real accounts are debited with additions, so a new van is debited to the motor vehicle account. The credit side is used for disposals, items damaged beyond use, or gifts given out. The van must be recorded when it is acquired, whether it is paid for at once or bought on credit.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: Equipment in a factory in Agbara is damaged beyond use in a fire. How is this recorded in the equipment (real) account?

options.a: The equipment account is debited and credited with the same amount
options.d: The equipment account is not affected

questions.explanation: Items damaged beyond use are recorded on the credit side of a real account, just like disposals, because the asset has left the business. Debiting the account would wrongly show an addition to equipment. Leaving the account unchanged would overstate the assets.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: Impersonal accounts are made up of
questions.explanation: Ledger accounts are classified principally into personal and impersonal accounts, and impersonal accounts are the real and nominal accounts together. Any group that includes personal accounts, such as customers and suppliers, cannot be impersonal.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: A cooperative society in Ibadan sorts its ledger accounts into personal and impersonal. Which account belongs with the personal accounts rather than the impersonal ones?

options.b: The account of a credit customer, Mrs Adeyemi

questions.explanation: A credit customer's account is a personal account, kept for a person, so it is not impersonal. The motor vehicle account is a real account, and the salaries and rent accounts are nominal accounts; real and nominal accounts together make up the impersonal accounts.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: Pick the set in which every account records a tangible thing owned by the business.
questions.explanation: Real accounts record tangible things, and cash, motor vehicles and goods are all tangible. Rent, salaries, electricity, discounts and wages are gains or losses and so are nominal accounts, and customers' accounts are personal, so each of the other groups is mixed.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: An accounting clerk is asked to group expense and income accounts together. Which set is made up entirely of nominal accounts?
questions.explanation: Rent, salaries and electricity are all expenses, which are gains and losses recorded in nominal accounts. Cash and land are tangible things kept in real accounts, and suppliers' accounts are personal, so each of the other groups contains a non-nominal account.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: A business keeps sales, purchases and general ledgers, among others. Which book listed below is NOT a ledger?
questions.explanation: The four types of ledger are the sales ledger, the purchases ledger, the general ledger, and the cash book with the petty cash book. The sales day book is a book of prime entry, not a ledger; its entries are posted to the sales ledger and the sales account.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: The accounts of the suppliers from whom a business buys goods on credit are kept in the
questions.explanation: Suppliers' accounts are kept in the purchases ledger, also called the payables or creditors ledger. The sales ledger is the tempting choice, but it holds the personal accounts of customers, not suppliers. The general ledger holds the nominal and real accounts.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: The sales ledger is also known as the
questions.explanation: The sales ledger holds customers' personal accounts, so it is also called the receivables or debtors ledger. The payables or creditors ledger is the purchases ledger, which holds suppliers' accounts, and the nominal ledger is another name for the general ledger.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: The general (nominal) ledger contains
questions.explanation: The general ledger holds nominal accounts such as expenses, wages, rent, sales and purchases, and real accounts such as land, buildings, vehicles, inventory and plant. Customers' accounts are in the sales ledger, suppliers' accounts in the purchases ledger, and cash and bank transactions in the cash book.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: In which ledger would a firm in Ikeja keep its land and buildings accounts?
questions.explanation: Land and buildings are real accounts, and real accounts are kept in the general ledger together with the nominal accounts. The sales and purchases ledgers hold personal accounts of customers and suppliers, and the petty cash book records small cash transactions.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: A business's wages account and bad debts account are kept in the
questions.explanation: Wages and bad debts are nominal accounts, which are kept in the general (nominal) ledger. The bad debts account may look linked to customers, but the customers' own accounts are in the sales ledger; the expense account itself is in the general ledger. The purchases ledger holds suppliers' accounts.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: A UNILAG department buys new office furniture for its staff room. The furniture account is best described as
questions.explanation: Furniture bought for use is a tangible asset of the department, so its account is a real account. It is not a nominal account, because it is not a gain or loss, and not a personal account, because it is not kept for a person. The purchases account is for goods bought for resale.

questions.topic: Ledger accounts and types of accounts
questions.question: In the books of a printing firm in Yaba, which of these accounts would be kept as a personal account?

options.b: The account of Femi Ventures, a credit customer

questions.explanation: Femi Ventures is a business customer buying on credit, and accounts for persons, companies or partnerships are personal accounts. Plant and machinery is a real account, while commission received and salaries are gains and losses recorded in nominal accounts.

questions.question: The cash book showed a debit balance of N1,000 in the bank column. On the same day, the bank statement showed a credit balance of N900. Which could be the reason for this difference?

options.a: Standing order for property tax paid directly by the bank
options.c: Direct credit received from a customer

questions.explanation: The bank balance (N900) is N100 lower than the cash book balance (N1,000), so the bank must have taken money out that the cash book has not recorded yet - a standing order paid directly by the bank does exactly that. Options B, C and D would all make the bank statement balance higher than the cash book, not lower.

questions.question: When preparing a bank reconciliation statement, which of the following is deducted from the balance as per bank statement?
questions.explanation: Unpresented cheques have already been deducted in the cash book but have not yet left the bank account, so they are deducted from the bank statement balance to arrive at the cash book balance. Option A, uncredited cheques, is added to the bank statement balance instead, while options C and D are corrections made in the cash book itself.

questions.question: In bank reconciliation, direct transfer is posted to where?

options.a: The credit side of cash book
options.b: The debit side of bank statement
options.c: The credit side of bank statement
options.d: The debit side of adjusted cash book

questions.explanation: A direct transfer into the business account is money already received by the bank but not yet recorded by the business, so it is entered on the debit (receipts) side when the cash book is adjusted. Option A would treat it as a payment, and options B and C refer to the bank's own statement, which already shows it.

questions.question: Where is an unpresented cheque found?

options.a: On the debit side of the cash book
options.b: On the credit side of the cash book
options.c: On the credit side of bank reconciliation
options.d: On the debit side of bank statement

questions.explanation: An unpresented cheque is one the business has written and recorded as a payment, so it sits on the credit (payments) side of the cash book, but the bank has not paid it yet. Option A is where receipts go, and option D is wrong because the bank has not yet recorded it at all.

questions.question: What is the effect of bank charges on adjusted cash book

options.a: It Reduces the adjusted cash book balance
options.c: It can increase or reduce the adjusted cash book balance
options.d: It increases the adjusted cash book balance

questions.explanation: Bank charges are money the bank has already taken from the account, so they are entered on the credit side of the cash book and reduce the adjusted cash book balance. Option D gets the direction wrong, and option C is wrong because charges can only reduce the balance.

questions.question: The discount values in the cashbook should, at an agreed period be

options.b: Deducted from respective cash balances in the cash book
options.c: Added to respective bank balances in the cash book
options.d: Transferred in total to their respective accounts

questions.explanation: The discount columns in a three-column cash book are memorandum columns, so their totals are transferred periodically to the discount allowed and discount received accounts in the ledger.
