Option A is wrong because the two discounts are separate items, and options B and C would mix discounts with real cash and bank balances.

questions.question: After the cash book has been updated (adjusted), which of the listed items are used to prepare the bank reconciliation statement? I Direct credit; II Error made by bank; III Dishonoured cheques; IV Error made by the cashier; V Uncredited cheques; VI Bank charges; VII Unpresented cheques
questions.explanation: A bank reconciliation statement shows the items that explain why the updated cash book and the bank statement still differ: errors made by the bank, uncredited cheques (lodgements not yet credited) and unpresented cheques. Direct credits, dishonoured cheques, bank charges and cashier errors are put right in the cash book first, which is why options A, B and C are wrong.

questions.question: The difference between the balance in a company's cash account and its bank statement is documented in the ____ of the bank statement.
questions.explanation: A bank reconciliation statement explains the differences between the cash book balance and the bank statement balance, such as unpresented cheques and lodgements not yet credited. Materiality (Option C) and conservatism (Option D) are accounting concepts, not documents that compare the two balances.

questions.question: Which of the following would not cause a difference between a bank statement and cash book

options.b: Book-keeping errors in cash book (bank column)
options.c: Bookkeeping errors in petty cash book

questions.explanation: The petty cash book records small cash payments and has nothing to do with the bank account, so its errors cannot cause a difference between the cash book (bank column) and the bank statement. Errors in the bank statement (Option A), errors in the bank column of the cash book (Option B) and direct debits not yet in the cash book (Option D) are all normal reasons for a difference.

questions.question: Which of the following items should not appear on the debit side of the bank statement?

options.a: Cheques issued by account holders and paid by the bank
options.d: Dividend received by the bank on behalf of the account holder

questions.explanation: The debit side of a bank statement shows money going out of the customer's account, such as cheques paid, direct debits and standing orders. A dividend collected by the bank for the customer increases the account, so it appears on the credit side. Options A, B and C are all withdrawals and correctly appear as debits.

questions.question: Which of the following may have been recorded in the cash book and yet fail to appear in the bank statement?

options.d: Payments made by the bank on standing order

questions.explanation: A lodgement entered in the cash book may not yet have been credited by the bank by the statement date, so it appears in the cash book but not on the bank statement. Option B is wrong because a cheque that has been presented and cashed has already passed through the bank account. Options A and D are the opposite case: the bank records them first, and they are often missing from the cash book.

questions.question: Which of the following items appearing on bank reconciliation would require an adjusting entry?
questions.explanation: Interest credited by the bank appears on the bank statement but is not yet in the cash book, so the business must make an entry to record it. Outstanding cheques (A) and uncredited cheques (B) are timing differences already correctly recorded in the cash book, and they clear on their own when the bank processes them. Option D is a result of the reconciliation, not an item needing an entry.

questions.question: A bank reconciliation statement explains the difference between which two balances?

options.a: The bank statement balance and the cash book (bank column) balance
options.b: The imprest and the cash book balance
options.c: The trial balance and the ledger balance

questions.explanation: A bank reconciliation statement explains why the balance on the bank statement differs from the bank column balance in the cash book, for example because of unpresented cheques or bank charges. Option B mentions the imprest, which belongs to petty cash, not the bank account. Option C describes the trial balance, which checks ledger balances and has nothing to do with the bank.

questions.question: A book showing statement of payment and receipt balances
questions.explanation: The cash book records cash and bank receipts on the debit side and payments on the credit side, and it is balanced off to show the cash and bank balances. A journal (B) is a book of prime entry for unusual transactions, and the ledger (C) contains accounts of all kinds, not specifically receipts and payments.

questions.question: In a bank reconciliation statement, which of the following would be added to the balance as per bank statement?
questions.explanation: Uncredited cheques (lodgements already entered in the cash book but not yet shown by the bank) are added to the bank statement balance to arrive at the cash book balance. Option C (outstanding or unpresented cheques) is deducted from the bank statement balance, not added. Options A and B are items that need to be entered in the cash book rather than adjusted on the bank statement balance.

questions.question: When is a petty cash account debited?

options.a: When the fund is established and every time money is spent
options.b: Every time money is drawn from the petty cash
options.c: When the fund is established and when the size of the float is decreased
options.d: When the fund is established and every time money is replenished

questions.explanation: Under the imprest system the petty cash account is debited when the float is first set up and each time it is topped up (reimbursed) to the original amount. Options A and B are wrong because spending petty cash is recorded on the credit side. Option C is wrong because reducing the float takes money out, which is a credit.

questions.question: Which of the following Items is not recorded in the cash book?
questions.explanation: Depreciation is a non-cash expense, so it never passes through the cash book; it is recorded through the journal. Bank charges, salaries and receipts from debtors (options A, C and D) all involve actual movements of money, so they are recorded in the cash book.

questions.question: A credit balance in the bank column of double column cash book is an Indication of

options.d: Surplus of cash in the bank

questions.explanation: In the cash book the debit side shows money coming in and the credit side money going out, so a credit balance in the bank column means more has been paid out than the business has in the bank: an overdraft. Options B and D describe a debit balance, and option C is wrong because the bank column has nothing to do with cash at hand.

questions.question: The unticked items on the debit side of the bank statement could be all of the following except
questions.explanation: Items on the debit side of the bank statement that are not yet in the cash book are amounts the bank has taken out of the account, such as direct debits, bank charges and dishonoured cheques (options A, B and D). A direct (credit) transfer is money paid into the account, so it appears on the credit side of the bank statement and is the exception.

questions.question: The cash book is said to be both a journal and a ledger because it

options.a: Lists the balances of all accounts at the end of the period
options.b: Records transactions as they happen, and double entry is completed in it
options.c: Records only credit transactions and their totals
options.d: Is prepared by the bank and checked by the business

questions.explanation: The cash book acts as a journal because transactions are written in it as they happen, and as a ledger because double entry is completed within it. It is kept by the business, not the bank, it records cash rather than credit transactions, and a list of balances is a trial balance.

questions.question: On which side of the cash book are receipts recorded?

options.d: Either side, depending on the amount

questions.explanation: The cash book is an asset account, so receipts, which increase cash or bank, go on the debit side and payments go on the credit side. The credit side is the tempting answer for anyone thinking from the bank statement's point of view, where lodgements are shown as credits.

questions.question: A trader in Balogun market pays N50,000 of office cash into the business bank account. How is this recorded in a two-column cash book?

options.a: As a contra entry: debit the bank column and credit the cash column
options.b: Debit the cash column and credit the bank column
options.c: Debit capital and credit the bank column
options.d: Debit the bank column only, with no other entry

questions.explanation: Moving money between cash and bank is a contra entry within the cash book: the bank column is debited because bank increases, and the cash column is credited because cash decreases. Debiting cash and crediting bank reverses the movement. Both sides must be recorded, and capital is not involved since the money stays in the business.

questions.question: A three-column cash book has money columns for
questions.explanation: The three-column cash book has columns for cash, bank and discount. The two-column cash book has only cash and bank, and the single-column cash book has just one of them. Petty cash is kept in a separate petty cash book.

questions.question: In a three-column cash book, discount allowed and discount received are recorded

options.a: Discount allowed on the credit side and discount received on the debit side
options.c: Discount allowed on the debit side and discount received on the credit side

questions.explanation: Discount allowed is given to customers when they pay, so it sits on the debit (receipts) side next to the money received. Discount received is given by suppliers when the business pays, so it sits on the credit (payments) side. Swapping the two is the common slip.

questions.question: On a bank statement, the credit column shows

options.a: Unpresented cheques issued by the customer
options.b: Bank charges deducted by the bank
options.c: Payments and withdrawals from the account

questions.explanation: The bank statement is the bank's record of the customer's account, which is a liability to the bank, so lodgements are shown in the credit column. Payments, withdrawals and bank charges are shown in the debit column. Unpresented cheques do not appear on the statement at all, because they have not yet reached the bank.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a reason for preparing a bank reconciliation statement?

options.a: To calculate the depreciation charge for the year
options.d: To highlight errors made by the bank

questions.explanation: A bank reconciliation statement is prepared to update the cash book, correct errors, detect and prevent fraud, and highlight bank errors. Depreciation is a year-end adjustment to non-current assets and has nothing to do with comparing the cash book with the bank statement.

questions.question: A cheque received from a customer has been entered on the debit side of the cash book but has not yet been credited by the bank. This is called
questions.explanation: An uncredited cheque has been received and debited in the cash book but not yet credited by the bank. An unpresented cheque is the opposite case: one the business has issued and credited in the cash book that the payee has not yet presented. A dishonoured cheque is one the paying bank refuses.

questions.question: A written instruction by a customer to the bank to pay a fixed sum regularly to a named payee is known as a
questions.explanation: A standing order is the customer's written instruction to the bank to pay a fixed amount regularly to a named payee, and it appears as a debit on the bank statement. A credit transfer is money paid directly into the account, which is the opposite direction. A pay-in slip is used to lodge money.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a reason for a bank to dishonour a cheque?

options.a: The amounts in words and figures differ
options.b: The cheque has an alteration that has not been endorsed
options.c: There are insufficient funds in the drawer's account
options.d: The cheque was paid into the bank on the same day it was received

questions.explanation: Paying a cheque in promptly is perfectly normal and gives the bank no reason to refuse it. Cheques are dishonoured for defects such as insufficient funds, an irregular or missing signature, words and figures that differ, no date or a post-dated cheque, or an unendorsed alteration.

questions.question: When the cash book is ticked against the bank statement, unticked items on the credit side of the cash book are
questions.explanation: The credit side of the cash book records payments, so an unticked credit is a cheque the business has issued that has not yet reached the bank: an unpresented cheque. Uncredited cheques are found among the unticked debits of the cash book, while credit transfers and standing orders are found among the unticked items on the bank statement.

questions.question: In preparing the adjusted (updated) cash book, a cheque from a customer that the bank has returned as dishonoured is

options.a: Debited to the adjusted cash book
options.b: Left out because it was already recorded as a receipt
options.c: Credited to the adjusted cash book
options.d: Added to the bank statement balance in the BRS

questions.explanation: The dishonoured cheque was earlier debited as a receipt, but the money never arrived, so it is credited in the adjusted cash book to reverse it. Debiting it would count the receipt twice. It belongs in the adjusted cash book, not the BRS, which contains only uncredited cheques, unpresented cheques and bank errors.

questions.question: A bank in Lagos collects a dividend directly for its customer and credits it to the customer's account. When the business prepares its adjusted cash book, the dividend is

options.a: Recorded only in the bank statement and never in the cash book
options.b: Credited to the adjusted cash book
options.c: Debited to the adjusted cash book
options.d: Deducted from the bank statement balance in the BRS

questions.explanation: A dividend received by the bank on the customer's behalf is a direct credit, which increases the business's bank balance, so it is debited to the adjusted cash book. Crediting it would reduce the balance. Once the cash book has been updated, the dividend does not need to appear in the BRS at all.

questions.question: Items that appear on the bank statement but not yet in the cash book include

options.b: Contra entries between cash and bank
options.d: Direct debits and direct credits, such as bank charges and credit transfers

questions.explanation: Items in the bank statement but not in the cash book are direct debits, such as standing orders and bank charges, and direct credits, such as credit transfers, dividends and interest. Uncredited and unpresented cheques are the reverse case: they are in the cash book but not yet in the bank statement.

questions.question: A firm's cash book shows a debit bank balance of N180,000. The bank statement reveals bank charges of N2,500, a standing order of N12,000, a credit transfer of N30,000 and a dishonoured cheque of N8,000, none yet in the cash book. What is the adjusted cash book balance?
questions.explanation: Add the credit transfer and deduct the bank charges, standing order and dishonoured cheque: 180,000 + 30,000 - 2,500 - 12,000 - 8,000 = N187,500. N195,500 forgets to deduct the dishonoured cheque, which reverses an earlier receipt. N157,500 leaves out the credit transfer, and N127,500 wrongly deducts it instead of adding it.

questions.question: A trader's adjusted cash book shows a debit balance of N187,500. There are unpresented cheques of N45,000 and uncredited cheques of N22,000. What balance should the bank statement show?
questions.explanation: Starting from the adjusted cash book, add back unpresented cheques and deduct uncredited cheques: 187,500 + 45,000 - 22,000 = N210,500. N164,500 reverses the two adjustments. N254,500 adds both items, forgetting that uncredited cheques are not yet in the bank balance.

questions.question: A business's cash book shows a bank overdraft of N40,000. The bank statement shows bank charges of N1,500 and a direct credit of N10,000, neither yet in the cash book. What is the adjusted cash book balance?
questions.explanation: Bank charges make the overdraft larger and the direct credit reduces it: 40,000 + 1,500 - 10,000 = N31,500 overdrawn. N51,500 treats the direct credit as if it increased the overdraft, and N48,500 adds the credit and deducts the charges the wrong way round. The account is still overdrawn because the credit is smaller than the overdraft.

questions.question: The bank statement of a shop in Ikeja shows a favourable balance of N95,000. Uncredited cheques total N18,000 and unpresented cheques total N27,500. Starting from the bank statement, what is the balance per cash book?
questions.explanation: Starting from the bank statement, add uncredited cheques and deduct unpresented cheques: 95,000 + 18,000 - 27,500 = N85,500. N104,500 reverses the two adjustments, and N140,500 adds both of them. Uncredited cheques are added because the cash book already includes them, while unpresented cheques are deducted because the cash book has already paid them out.

questions.question: In a bank reconciliation statement, how is an overdrawn balance usually shown?

options.a: In red ink with no sign
options.b: As a positive figure in a separate column
options.c: As a footnote below the statement

questions.explanation: An overdraft is an abnormal balance, and in a bank reconciliation statement overdrawn balances are shown in brackets, for example (32,500). Showing it as a plain positive figure would make it look like money in the bank, and a footnote would leave it out of the calculation.

questions.question: When preparing a bank reconciliation statement, which balances are compared?

options.a: The petty cash book and the bank statement
options.b: The cash column of the cash book and the opening balance on the bank statement
options.c: The discount columns and the bank statement
options.d: The bank column of the cash book and the closing balance on the bank statement

questions.explanation: The comparison is always between the bank column of the cash book and the bank statement, using the closing bank-statement balance. The cash column records physical cash held by the business, and the petty cash book and discount columns are not part of the bank account at all.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: Trial balance could be used to

options.a: Check accuracy of postings to ledger
options.c: To detect errors in the ledger

questions.explanation: A trial balance lists every ledger balance to check that total debits equal total credits, which confirms the arithmetical accuracy of the postings to the ledger. Option C is partly true, but many errors, such as errors of omission or principle, leave the trial balance in agreement, so checking accuracy is the best answer. Option B is wrong because a trial balance does not correct anything by itself.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: A listing of the balances in the accounts in order to determine whether debits are equal to credits is a ____ balance.
questions.explanation: A trial balance lists the balances on all ledger accounts to check that total debits equal total credits. The journal (Option B) is a book of original entry, the balance sheet (Option C) reports financial position, and a chart of accounts (Option D) only lists account names.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: ___ is a statement which lists all the debit and credit balances of an organization
questions.explanation: A trial balance lists all the debit and credit balances from the ledger accounts at a date, to check that total debits equal total credits. A suspense account (option A) only holds a difference temporarily. The trading account (option D) and the profit and loss account (option C) use some of these balances to work out profit, but they do not list all of them.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: In trial balance, all expenses are treated in the ___
questions.explanation: Expenses have debit balances in the ledger, so they appear on the debit side of the trial balance. The credit side (A) holds incomes, liabilities and capital. Option C is wrong because an expense balance cannot be on both sides.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: Which of the following best describes a trial balance?

options.a: A list of all debit and credit balances extracted from the ledger at the end of a period
options.b: A record of transactions in date order before they are posted to the ledger
options.c: A statement comparing the cash book balance with the bank statement balance
options.d: A statement showing the profit or loss made by a business for a period

questions.explanation: A trial balance is a schedule of every debit and credit balance taken from the ledger at the end of a period, and its two column totals are expected to agree. A record of transactions in date order before posting describes a book of prime entry such as the journal, which comes before the ledger, not after it.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: Because it brings every ledger balance together in one schedule, a trial balance is often described as a
questions.explanation: A trial balance simply summarises the balances already sitting in the ledger accounts, which is why it is called a summary of ledger balances. A book of original entry is where transactions are first recorded before they ever reach the ledger, so it cannot be a summary of ledger balances.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: The main purpose of extracting a trial balance is to

options.a: Show how much the business owes its bank at the year end
options.b: Confirm that the general ledger entries are balanced
options.c: Show the profit earned by the business for the year
options.d: Record transactions before they are posted to the ledger

questions.explanation: A trial balance checks whether total debit balances equal total credit balances, which confirms that the general ledger entries are balanced. Showing the profit for the year is the job of the income statement, which is prepared later using the trial balance figures.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: Which of the following is the correct heading for the trial balance of Femi Traders, Balogun market?

options.b: Trial Balance for the year ended 31 December 2025
options.d: Trial Balance for the period ended 31 December 2025

questions.explanation: A trial balance lists the balances on the ledger accounts at one particular date, so its heading uses "as at" followed by that date. "For the year ended" describes a statement that covers a whole period, such as the income statement, so it does not suit a list of balances taken at a point in time.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: When a bookkeeper in Balogun market extracts a trial balance, the figure taken from each ledger account is the

options.a: Largest single entry in the account
options.b: Opening balance at the start of the year
options.c: Total of the debit side of the account

questions.explanation: Each ledger account is balanced off, and the balance brought down (bal b/d) is the figure listed in the trial balance. Using the total of the debit side would ignore the credit entries in the account and would not give the account's balance.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: A trial balance extracted from the ledger before any end-of-year adjustments have been made is called
questions.explanation: Before items like accruals, prepayments and depreciation are adjusted for, the list of ledger balances is an unadjusted trial balance. An adjusted trial balance is the version prepared after those year-end adjustments have been put through, so it does not fit the description.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: All but one of these are uses of a trial balance. Identify the exception.

options.a: It serves as the basis for preparing the final accounts
options.b: It checks the accuracy of postings and extraction
options.c: It helps auditors in their work
options.d: It proves that the ledger contains no errors at all

questions.explanation: A trial balance whose totals agree only shows that debits equal credits; some errors, such as an error of omission, leave the totals in agreement, so it cannot prove the ledger is error-free. Checking the accuracy of postings and extraction is a genuine use, because a disagreement points to a posting or extraction mistake.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: A trial balance is said to give a "bird's eye view" of the books. This means it

options.a: Shows the cash position as confirmed by the bank
options.b: Lists transactions in the order in which they occurred
options.c: Shows the detailed entries in each ledger account
options.d: Gives an overview of all the ledger balances at a glance

questions.explanation: Like a view from above, a trial balance shows all the ledger balances together on one page, giving a quick overview of the books. It does not show the detailed entries inside each account; those are found only in the ledger accounts themselves.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: Extracting a trial balance is important for several reasons. Which of these is not among them?

options.a: It eases the preparation of the final accounts
options.b: It checks the arithmetical accuracy of the ledger
options.c: It records transactions in the order in which they occur

questions.explanation: Recording transactions in date order is the job of the books of prime entry, such as the journal and day books, not the trial balance. Checking the arithmetical accuracy of the ledger is a real importance of the trial balance, since it tests whether total debits equal total credits.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: The manager of a firm in Ikeja uses the figures in this year's trial balance to help draw up next year's spending plan. Which importance of the trial balance does this illustrate?

options.b: It helps prepare the audit report
options.c: It checks the arithmetical accuracy of the ledger

questions.explanation: Using trial balance figures to plan future spending is an example of the trial balance aiding budgets and decision-making. Rectifying ledger errors is a different importance: it is about finding and correcting mistakes, not planning ahead.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: The accountant of a UNILAG cooperative shop places this year's trial balance beside last year's to see how each expense has changed. This use of the trial balance is best described as
questions.explanation: Setting the figures of two years side by side to spot changes is comparative analysis, one of the stated importances of a trial balance. Checking arithmetical accuracy is about whether debits equal credits in one trial balance, not about comparing years.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: Once a trial balance has been extracted and agrees, it is mainly used as the basis for preparing
questions.explanation: The balances in an agreed trial balance are used to prepare the final accounts, that is, the income statement and the statement of financial position. Invoices, receipts, the books of prime entry and the ledger all come before the trial balance in the accounting process, so they cannot be prepared from it.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: In a trial balance, which of the following balances is shown in the credit column?
questions.explanation: Capital is what the business owes its owner, so it is a credit balance in the trial balance. Drawings are a debit balance because they are recorded as Dr drawings when the owner takes value out of the business, which reduces capital.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: Which of the following balances would appear in the debit column of a trial balance?
questions.explanation: Expenses are debit balances, so rent expense goes in the debit column. Sales is income and is therefore a credit balance, while a bank loan is a liability and capital is owed to the owner, both shown as credits.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: In a trial balance, the balance on a Commission received account is shown

options.a: In the debit column, because it is an asset
options.b: In the credit column, because it is income
options.c: In the credit column, because it is a liability
options.d: In the debit column, because it is income

questions.explanation: Commission received is income earned by the business, and income balances are credits in a trial balance. Placing it in the debit column because it is income gets the rule backwards: it is expenses, not income, that are debits.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: A balance of N45,000 on the Prepaid insurance account appears in the trial balance as a

options.a: Credit, because it is a liability
options.b: Debit, because it is an asset
options.d: Debit, because it is an expense owing

questions.explanation: Prepaid insurance is a payment made in advance for cover not yet used, so it is an asset and assets are debit balances. Treating it as a liability confuses it with an amount owing, such as salary payable, which would be a credit.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: Which pair of balances is correctly placed in a trial balance?

options.a: Discounts received - debit; bad debts - debit
options.b: Discounts received - credit; bad debts - credit
options.c: Discounts received - debit; bad debts - credit
options.d: Discounts received - credit; bad debts - debit

questions.explanation: Discounts received are a gain to the business, so they are a credit balance, while bad debts are an expense and therefore a debit balance. The pair with both as debits wrongly treats discounts received as a cost, when they actually reduce what the business pays.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: At the year end, a trader's ledger shows balances for prepaid insurance, salaries expense, salary payable and cash in hand. Which of these is a credit balance in the trial balance?
questions.explanation: Salary payable is salary owed to staff but not yet paid, which is a liability and therefore a credit balance. Salaries expense is a tempting choice, but it is an expense, and expenses are debit balances.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: Rent receivable of N5,000, being rent earned by the business but not yet received at the year end, appears in the trial balance as a

options.a: Debit balance, because it is an expense
options.b: Debit balance, because it is an asset
options.c: Credit balance, because it is a liability
options.d: Credit balance, because it is income

questions.explanation: Rent that has been earned but not yet received is accrued income, an amount owed to the business, so it is an asset and a debit balance. The rent income itself is a credit in the income account, but the receivable balance is the asset side of that entry, so calling the receivable a credit is wrong.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: Which of the following statements about a trial balance whose two totals agree is correct?

options.a: The ledger is free from all errors
options.b: Every transaction must have been recorded at the correct amount
options.c: No transaction can have been posted to the wrong account
options.d: Errors may still exist in the ledger even though the totals agree

questions.explanation: Agreement only shows that total debits equal total credits, and some errors, such as omissions or postings to the wrong account, leave the totals equal. Saying the ledger is free from all errors goes too far, because those errors would not show up as a difference.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: Errors discovered in the ledger are corrected by first recording the correcting entries in the
questions.explanation: The journal is the book of prime entry used for unusual entries, including the correction of errors, before they are posted to the ledger. The cash book records cash and bank receipts and payments, not corrections.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: Which of the following errors does NOT affect the agreement of the trial balance totals?

options.a: Adding up one ledger account incorrectly
options.b: Listing a debit balance in the credit column of the trial balance
options.d: Posting only the debit side of a transaction

questions.explanation: In an error of complete reversal, the correct accounts are used but the debit and credit are swapped, so equal amounts still appear on both sides and the totals agree. Posting only the debit side of a transaction leaves the debits larger than the credits, so it does cause a difference.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: Pick the group in which every error leaves the debit and credit totals of the trial balance equal.

options.a: Original entry, complete reversal and compensating errors
options.b: Original entry, single entry and casting errors
options.c: Compensating, one-sided posting and casting errors
options.d: Principle, single entry and complete reversal

questions.explanation: Errors of original entry, complete reversal and compensating errors all leave equal amounts on the debit and credit sides, so the trial balance still agrees. Any list containing a single entry or one-sided posting is wrong, because posting only one side of a transaction makes the totals differ.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: When the two totals of a trial balance do not agree, the difference is temporarily entered in a
questions.explanation: A suspense account holds the difference in a trial balance until the errors causing it are found and corrected through the journal. Putting the difference in the capital account would hide the error inside the owner's balance instead of tracking it for correction.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: Chika Ventures, Ikeja, had the following balances at 31 December 2025: Capital N400,000; Equipment N250,000; Purchases N180,000; Sales N320,000; Trade payables N60,000; Trade receivables N90,000; Rent expense N40,000; Cash at bank N220,000. What is the total of the debit column of the trial balance?
questions.explanation: The debit balances are the assets and expenses: 250,000 + 180,000 + 90,000 + 40,000 + 220,000 = N780,000, which equals the credits of 400,000 + 320,000 + 60,000. N840,000 comes from wrongly treating trade payables, a liability, as a debit.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: The ledger of Mama Nkechi's provision store shows: Cash N35,000; Inventory N120,000; Furniture N80,000; Purchases N200,000; Wages N45,000; Sales N310,000; Trade payables N50,000; and Capital (balance missing). If the trial balance agrees, what is the capital balance?
questions.explanation: Debits are 35,000 + 120,000 + 80,000 + 200,000 + 45,000 = N480,000, and the known credits are 310,000 + 50,000 = N360,000, so capital must be 480,000 - 360,000 = N120,000. N220,000 results from placing trade payables in the debit column, but payables are a liability and belong on the credit side.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: A trial balance shows a debit total of N1,245,000 and a credit total of N1,230,000. To make the totals agree while the errors are investigated, a suspense account is opened with
questions.explanation: The credit column is short by 1,245,000 - 1,230,000 = N15,000, so the suspense entry of N15,000 goes on the credit side to bring it up to the debit total. Entering it on the debit side would widen the gap to N30,000 instead of closing it.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: When the bookkeeper of a UNILAG student cooperative added up her trial balance, the credit column came to N684,800 and the debit column to N680,000. The suspense account needed to balance it is
questions.explanation: The debit column is N4,800 lower than the credit column (684,800 - 680,000), so a debit of N4,800 is placed in the suspense account to make the totals agree. A credit entry would push the credit side even higher and double the difference.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: A Lagos trading firm's balances are: Capital N1,000,000; Bank loan N500,000; Sales N1,800,000; Discounts received N20,000; Trade payables N180,000; Premises N900,000; Purchases N1,100,000; Salaries N300,000; Bad debts N15,000; Trade receivables N250,000; Bank N935,000. What is the total of the credit column of the trial balance?
questions.explanation: The credit balances are capital, the loan, sales, discounts received and payables: 1,000,000 + 500,000 + 1,800,000 + 20,000 + 180,000 = N3,500,000, which matches the debit total. N3,480,000 comes from wrongly treating discounts received as a debit, when it is a gain and therefore a credit.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: A trader's trial balance includes: Capital N600,000; Sales N450,000; Trade payables N70,000; Machinery N400,000; Purchases N300,000; Trade receivables N85,000; Carriage inwards N15,000; Drawings N40,000; and Cash (balance missing). If the trial balance agrees, what is the cash balance?
questions.explanation: Credits total 600,000 + 450,000 + 70,000 = N1,120,000, and the known debits total 400,000 + 300,000 + 85,000 + 15,000 + 40,000 = N840,000, so cash is 1,120,000 - 840,000 = N280,000. N360,000 comes from treating drawings as a credit, but drawings are a debit because they reduce what the business owes the owner.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: A credit sale of N25,000 to Bola was correctly debited to Bola's account, but no entry was made in the sales account. What effect does this have on the trial balance?

options.a: The debit total exceeds the credit total by N50,000
options.c: The debit total exceeds the credit total by N25,000
options.d: The credit total exceeds the debit total by N25,000

questions.explanation: Only the debit side of the transaction was posted, so the debit column is N25,000 larger than the credit column, and the difference would go to a suspense account. The totals cannot still agree, because one side of the double entry is missing.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: A rent payment of N8,000 was credited in the bank account and also credited, instead of debited, in the rent account. What effect does this have on the trial balance?

options.a: The debit total exceeds the credit total by N8,000
options.c: The credit total exceeds the debit total by N8,000
options.d: The credit total exceeds the debit total by N16,000

questions.explanation: The rent account should have had a debit of N8,000 but got a credit of N8,000 instead, so the credits are N8,000 too high and the debits N8,000 too low, a total gap of N16,000. Saying the gap is only N8,000 forgets that the missing debit and the extra credit both widen the difference.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: The purchases balance of N50,000 was entered in the credit column of a trial balance instead of the debit column. Assuming no other errors, the trial balance will show
questions.explanation: Purchases is an expense and belongs in the debit column, so moving it to the credit side makes credits N50,000 too high and debits N50,000 too low, a difference of N100,000. A gap of only N50,000 counts just one of the two effects.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: Which of the following correctly states where items are placed in a trial balance?

options.a: Assets and capital in the debit column; liabilities, expenses and income in the credit column
options.b: Assets and expenses in the debit column; liabilities, capital and income in the credit column
options.c: Expenses and liabilities in the debit column; assets, capital and income in the credit column
options.d: Assets and income in the debit column; liabilities, capital and expenses in the credit column

questions.explanation: Assets and expenses are debit balances, while liabilities, capital and income are credit balances, and this is how the two columns are filled. The option placing income in the debit column is wrong because income, such as sales, is always a credit balance.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: A trial balance laid out with the columns Narration, Debit (N) and Credit (N) uses the Narration column to show

options.a: The name of each ledger account
options.b: The folio reference of each posting
options.d: The explanation of each journal entry

questions.explanation: The Narration (or Particulars) column lists the name of each ledger account whose balance is shown in the Debit or Credit column beside it. A folio reference is not shown, because this layout has no folio column at all.

questions.topic: Trial balance and correction of errors
questions.question: At what stage of the accounting process is a trial balance normally extracted?

options.a: Only when an external audit is being carried out
options.b: At the end of a period, after transactions have been posted to the ledger
options.c: Each time a single transaction is recorded
options.d: Before transactions are recorded in the books of prime entry

questions.explanation: A trial balance is drawn up at the end of a period from the balances already posted in the ledger. It cannot come before the books of prime entry, because there would be no ledger balances to list yet.

questions.question: Which one of the following is the correct entry for unsold stock at the end of the accounting period?

options.b: Debit cost of sales; credit inventory
options.c: Debit profit or loss; credit inventory
options.d: Debit inventory; credit cost of sales

questions.explanation: Unsold stock at the year end is an asset carried into the next period, so inventory is debited and cost of sales is credited, which cuts cost of sales down to the cost of the goods actually sold. Option A is wrong because closing stock has not been sold, so it is never added to sales revenue. Options B and C reverse the entry by crediting inventory.

questions.question: What type of entry will increase the normal balance of the general ledger account that reports the amount owed as of the balance sheet date for a company's accrued expenses?
questions.explanation: Accrued expenses owed at the balance sheet date are recorded in a liability account, and liabilities have normal credit balances, so a credit entry increases them. A debit (Option C) would reduce the liability, and Options A and B are account types, not entry types.

questions.question: What type of accounts are Interest Receivable and Fees Receivable?
questions.explanation: Interest receivable and fees receivable are amounts other people owe the business, so they are assets (usually current assets). They are not liabilities (Option B), which are amounts the business owes, and they are not revenue (Option D), even though they arise from earning interest or fees.

questions.question: What type of entry will decrease the normal balances of the accounts Deferred Revenues and Unearned Revenues?
questions.explanation: Deferred or unearned revenues are liabilities, which normally carry credit balances, so they are decreased by a debit entry (for example when the revenue is earned). Option D, a credit, would increase the liability. Options A and B are account types, not entry types.

questions.question: A ____ entry typically removes an accrual-type adjusting entry that had been recorded in the preceding accounting period.
questions.explanation: A reversing entry is made at the start of a new period to cancel an accrual adjustment from the previous period, so that the later cash payment or receipt can be recorded normally. A reconciliation (Option A) compares two records, such as the cash book and bank statement, and does not remove adjustments.

questions.question: What type of accounts are Deferred Revenues and Unearned Revenues?
questions.explanation: Deferred or unearned revenues are amounts received before the work is done, so the business owes the customer goods or services - that is a liability. Option A, asset, is a common mix-up with prepaid expenses, which are amounts the business has paid in advance. Option D is wrong because the revenue has not yet been earned.

questions.question: What type of accounts are Prepaid Insurance, Prepaid Advertising, and Prepaid Expenses?
questions.explanation: Prepaid insurance, prepaid advertising and other prepaid expenses are payments made for future benefits that the business still has the right to receive, so they are assets. Option D, expense, is tempting, but the cost only becomes an expense as the period passes. They are not liabilities (Option B) because nothing is owed by the business.

questions.question: What type of entry will decrease the normal balances of the accounts Prepaid Insurance and Prepaid Expenses, and Insurance Expense?
questions.explanation: Prepaid insurance and prepaid expenses are assets, and insurance expense is an expense; both kinds of account have normal debit balances, so a credit entry decreases them. A debit (Option B) would increase them, and Options A and D are account types, not entry types.

questions.question: The adjusting entry that reduces the balance in Deferred Revenues or Unearned Revenues will also include which of the following?
questions.explanation: When unearned revenue becomes earned, the liability is debited (reduced) and a revenue account such as Fees Earned is credited. Option C, a debit to fees earned, reverses the correct side, and Option A involves cash, which was received earlier and is not part of the adjustment.

questions.question: The adjusting entry that reduces the balance in Prepaid Insurance will also include which of the following?
questions.explanation: As insurance is used up, the adjusting entry is DR Insurance Expense and CR Prepaid Insurance, which moves the expired part from an asset to an expense. Option B puts insurance expense on the wrong side, and Option A wrongly involves cash, because the premium was already paid when the prepayment was set up.

questions.question: In the case of a company's deferred revenues, which occurs first?

options.b: Receiving The Money From The Customer

questions.explanation: Deferred (unearned) revenue arises when the customer pays before the business does the work, so receiving the money comes first and earning the revenue comes later. Option A describes accrued revenue, where the revenue is earned first and paid for later. Options C and D relate to interest and do not describe deferred revenues.

questions.question: In the case of a bank's accrued interest revenues, which occurs first?

options.a: Paying The Interest To The Lender
options.c: Receiving The Interest From The Borrower

questions.explanation: Accrued interest revenue means the bank has earned the interest but has not yet received it, so earning the revenue comes first and receiving the cash comes later. Option C, receiving the interest, happens after the revenue is earned, and Options A and D describe the borrower's side, not the bank's revenue.

questions.question: The ending balance in the account Prepaid Insurance is expected to report which of the following?

options.a: The Accrued Amount Of Insurance Expense
options.b: The Original Amount Of The Insurance Premiums Paid
options.c: The Expired Portion Of The Insurance Premiums Paid
options.d: The Unexpired Portion Of The Insurance Premiums Paid

questions.explanation: Prepaid insurance is an asset representing insurance paid for in advance that has not yet been used up, so its ending balance is the unexpired portion. Option C, the expired portion, has become insurance expense in the profit or loss account. Option B is the full premium, which would only equal the balance before any of it expires.

questions.question: Which of the following will be included in the adjusting entry to accrue interest income or interest revenues?
questions.explanation: To accrue interest income that has been earned but not yet received, the entry is debit Interest Receivable (an asset) and credit Interest Income. Option C has the receivable on the wrong side, and Option B debits income instead of crediting it. Option A is wrong because no cash has been received yet.

questions.question: In the case of a company deferring insurance expense, which occurs first?
questions.explanation: A deferred (prepaid) insurance expense arises when the company pays the insurer in advance, so the payment comes first and the expense is incurred later as the cover is used up. Option A describes the order for an accrued expense, where the cost is incurred before it is paid. Options C and D relate to fees revenue, not insurance expense.

questions.question: In the case of a company's accrued interest expense, which of the following occurs first?

options.b: Paying The Interest To The Lender
options.d: Receiving The Interest From The Borrower

questions.explanation: With an accrued interest expense, the company incurs the interest first and pays the lender later, which is why a liability (interest payable) is recorded at the year end. Option B, paying the lender, comes after the expense is incurred. Options A and D relate to the lender's side, where interest is earned or received, not to the borrower's expense.

questions.question: Which of the following will be included in the adjusting entry to accrue interest expense?
questions.explanation: To accrue interest expense that has been incurred but not yet paid, the entry is debit Interest Expense and credit Interest Payable (a liability). Option C puts Interest Payable on the wrong side; debiting it happens later, when the interest is paid. Option A is wrong because no cash has been paid yet, and Option D relates to interest paid in advance.

questions.question: Prepaid rent given in the Trial Balance will be treated as a:
questions.explanation: Prepaid rent is rent paid now for a future period, so the business has a benefit still to come, which makes it a current asset (a deferred expense). Option B (deferred income) and option C (liability) describe rent received in advance from someone else, and option D is wrong because paying rent is never revenue.

questions.question: When Rent receivable A/c is debited, the double entry effect of this transaction signifies

options.b: A null effect to the a/c
options.d: A stall effect to the a/c

questions.explanation: Rent receivable is an asset (income earned but not yet received), and assets increase on the debit side, so debiting it signifies an increase. Option C would be right only for a credit entry, while options B and D do not describe any real double entry effect.

questions.question: End of year adjustments are made in order to satisfy the
questions.explanation: Year-end adjustments such as accruals, prepayments, depreciation and provisions make sure income and expenses are matched to the period they belong to, which is the matching concept. Option B (consistency) is about using the same methods each year, and option D (going concern) is about the business continuing. There is no 'adjustment concept' (option A).

questions.question: If the accrued wages of a business amounting to N1800 is not recorded then

options.a: It is a liability, hence will overstate liability by N1,800
options.b: The profit will be over-stated by N1,800 and liabilities understated by N1,800
options.c: The profit will be under-stated by N1,800 and cash will be overstated by N1,800
options.d: The profit will be under-stated by N1,800 and liabilities overstated by N1,800

questions.explanation: Accrued wages are an expense owed at the year end; if they are left out, expenses are too low by N1,800, so profit is overstated by N1,800, and the amount owed is missing, so liabilities are understated by N1,800. The options saying profit is understated have the effect the wrong way round, and leaving out an accrual cannot overstate liabilities.

questions.question: During the year ended 31st December 20X2 the proprietor of a business had the following transactions with the business: Salaries received N100,000, Cash drawn to pay school fees N10,000, Withdrew goods worth N2,400 from the business. Half of this went towards the Xmas of the children while the balance was used as gifts to long standing customers of the business. From the above the total amount relevant as business expense is
questions.explanation: Only the goods given as gifts to long-standing customers are a business expense: half of N2,400 = N1,200. The owner's salary, school fees and the goods used for the children's Christmas are all drawings because they benefit the owner personally. Option D (N101,200) wrongly treats the owner's salary as a business expense.

questions.question: During the year ended 31st December 20X2 the proprietor of a business had the following transactions with the business: Salaries received N100,000, Cash drawn to pay school fees N10,000, Withdrew goods worth N2,400 from the business. Half of this went towards the Xmas of the children while the balance was used as gifts to long standing customers of the business. The total of the drawings of the proprietor is
questions.explanation: Drawings are everything the owner takes out for personal use: salary taken N100,000 + school fees N10,000 + half the goods N1,200 = N111,200. Option A (N112,400) includes all the goods, but the half given to customers is a business expense, not drawings. Option D (N101,200) leaves out the school fees.

questions.question: Which of the following accounts is not an asset?
questions.explanation: Rent received in advance is money received for a period not yet covered, so the business owes that service and it is a liability. Prepaid rent, prepaid insurance and accrued rent received (options A, B and D) are all amounts the business is owed or has paid ahead, which makes them assets.

questions.question: Given the following information, what is the rent for the period 2020. Rent paid in advance (31/12/2019): N1,000; Rent paid during the year 2020: N8,000; Rent owing (31/12/2020): N600
questions.explanation: Rent for 2020 = opening prepayment + paid during the year + closing amount owing = N1,000 + N8,000 + N600 = N9,600. Option C (N9,000) leaves out the rent owing at the year end, and option A (N8,600) ignores the opening prepayment.

questions.question: Electricity bill remaining unpaid as at the year-end should be accounted for as:

options.a: Dr. Electricity account and Cr. Cash account
options.b: Dr. Electricity accrued account and Cr. Electricity current account
options.c: Dr. Electricity account and Cr. Electricity accrued account
options.d: Dr. Pre-paid electricity account and Cr. Electricity account

questions.explanation: An unpaid electricity bill is an accrued expense: debit the electricity account to charge the expense this year and credit an accrual (liability) account to show the amount owed. Option A is wrong because no cash has been paid yet, and option D records a prepayment, which is the opposite situation.

questions.question: Rent and rates are N6,000 and Insurance N1,500. If a further N500 rent needs to be accrued and N250 of insurance is prepaid, what balances need to be shown in the profit and loss account?
questions.explanation: An accrual adds to the expense, so rent = N6,000 + N500 = N6,500; a prepayment reduces it, so insurance = N1,500 - N250 = N1,250. Option A adds the insurance prepayment instead of deducting it, and options B and D deduct the rent accrual instead of adding it.

questions.question: End-of-year adjustments are best described as

options.a: Amendments made at the end of a financial period in the income statement and statement of financial position so that the accounts show a true view
options.b: Corrections made in the cash book after comparing it with the bank statement at the end of each month
options.c: Entries made in the journal to record the capital introduced when the business first starts trading
options.d: Changes made to the trial balance figures only to force its debit and credit totals to agree

questions.explanation: End-of-year adjustments are amendments made at the end of each financial period to the income statement and the statement of financial position, so that the accounts give a true view. Changing figures just to force the trial balance to agree is not an adjustment; differences of that kind go to a suspense account until the errors are found.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a reason for making end-of-year adjustments?

options.a: To provide for depreciation of fixed assets
options.b: To reduce the amount of tax the business pays
options.c: To record all income generated in the year

questions.explanation: Adjustments are made so that the accounts follow accepted principles and show a true view, such as valuing closing stock, providing for depreciation and recording all income earned. Reducing tax is not a purpose of adjustments; recording all income generated in the year may even raise profit.

questions.question: The idea that revenue and expenditure should be recorded in the period to which they relate, not the period in which cash is received or paid, is known as the
questions.explanation: The accruals concept matches income and expenses to the period they belong to, regardless of when the cash moves. The going concern concept is about assuming the business will continue operating in the foreseeable future, which says nothing about the timing of income and expenses.

questions.question: An agent in Ikeja earned commission of N35,000 for work done in December 2025 but will not receive the money until January 2026. In the accounts for the year ended 31 December 2025, the N35,000 is

options.a: An accrued expense, shown as a current liability
options.b: A prepaid expense, shown as a current asset
options.c: Accrued income, shown as a current asset
options.d: Income received in advance, shown as a current liability

questions.explanation: Income that has been earned but not yet received at the year end is accrued income, and because it is owed to the business it is a current asset. Income received in advance is the opposite case, where cash comes in before the income is earned, so it is a liability.

questions.question: A business received commission of N45,000 in cash during 2025. Commission receivable was N6,000 at 1 January 2025 and N9,000 at 31 December 2025. What commission income should be credited to the income statement for 2025?
questions.explanation: Income for the year = received - opening accrual + closing accrual = 45,000 - 6,000 + 9,000 = N48,000. N42,000 reverses the two adjustments, adding the opening accrual and deducting the closing one.

questions.question: A firm paid motor expenses of N72,000 during the year. Motor expenses owing were N8,000 at the start of the year and N11,500 at the end of the year. What is the motor expenses charge in the income statement?
questions.explanation: Expense charge = paid - opening accrual + closing accrual = 72,000 - 8,000 + 11,500 = N75,500. N68,500 swaps the adjustments by adding the opening accrual and deducting the closing accrual.

questions.question: A trader in Balogun market paid insurance of N36,000 during the year. Insurance prepaid was N4,000 at the start of the year and N9,000 at the end of the year. What insurance expense should appear in the income statement?
questions.explanation: Expense charge = paid + opening prepayment - closing prepayment = 36,000 + 4,000 - 9,000 = N31,000. N23,000 wrongly deducts the opening prepayment as well, but last year's prepayment is cover used up this year and must be added.

questions.question: A UNILAG department lets out its hall and received rent of N120,000 during the year. Rent received in advance was N15,000 at the start of the year and N20,000 at the end of the year. What rent income should be credited to the income statement for the year?
questions.explanation: Income credited = received + opening income in advance - closing income in advance = 120,000 + 15,000 - 20,000 = N115,000. N125,000 swaps the two figures, but the closing amount received in advance belongs to next year and must be deducted.

questions.question: On 1 April 2025, a firm paid N480,000 for insurance cover for 2 years. If its year ends on 31 December 2025, how much of the payment is a prepayment in the statement of financial position at that date?
questions.explanation: The cover runs for 24 months, and 9 months (April to December) are used in 2025, so 15/24 x 480,000 = N300,000 is prepaid at the year end. N180,000 is the 9/24 share that is charged as an expense for 2025, not the amount still prepaid.

questions.question: A business paid electricity of N50,000 during the year. At the start of the year N4,000 was owing for electricity, and at the end of the year N3,000 had been paid in advance. What is the electricity charge for the year?
questions.explanation: Expense charge = paid - opening accrual - closing prepayment = 50,000 - 4,000 - 3,000 = N43,000. N51,000 adds the opening accrual instead of deducting it, but that N4,000 related to last year's electricity and was already charged then.

questions.question: Mr Okon, who owns a shop in Ikeja, takes N20,000 from the business cash till for his personal use. The correct entry is
questions.explanation: Cash taken by the owner for private use is debited to the drawings account and credited to cash, and the drawings are later deducted from capital. Debiting wages expense is wrong because the owner's withdrawal is not a business expense.

questions.question: Wages of N18,000 for the last week of December 2025 were not paid until 5 January 2026. In the statement of financial position at 31 December 2025, the N18,000 is shown as
questions.explanation: The wages were incurred in 2025 but were still unpaid at the year end, so they are an accrued expense, which is a current liability. A prepaid expense is the reverse situation, where payment is made before the expense is incurred.

questions.question: A motor van was bought for $20,000 on 1 September 2005 with a residual value of $2,000. Depreciation was charged at 20% by the reducing balance method on yearly basis. It was sold for $18,000 after three years of use on 30 September 2008. Compute the profit on sale of asset.
questions.explanation: Under 20% reducing balance, the net book value after three years is $20,000 x 0.8 x 0.8 x 0.8 = $10,240 (depreciation of $4,000, $3,200 and $2,560). Profit on sale = $18,000 - $10,240 = $7,760. The residual value is not used in the reducing balance calculation here, so the smaller options come from wrong bases.

questions.question: If an asset has original cost of N100,000, a useful life of 5 years and a salvage value of zero, what is the depreciation charge for the first year using the sum of the year digits.
questions.explanation: With a 5-year life, the sum of the years' digits is 1+2+3+4+5 = 15, and the first year takes 5/15 of the cost: 5/15 x N100,000 = N33,333.33. Option B, N20,000, is the straight-line charge (N100,000 / 5), which is a different method.

questions.question: What would be the accounting treatment for a cheque of N1,254,000 received for the disposal of a Plant and Machinery Item?

options.a: Debit Bank Account, Credit Accumulated Depreciation Account with N1,254,000
options.b: Debit Bank Account, Credit Asset Disposal Account with N1,254,000
options.c: Debit Bank Account, Credit Plant and Machinery Account with N1,254,000
options.d: Debit Asset Disposal Account, Credit Bank Account

questions.explanation: Disposal proceeds are recorded by debiting bank (money received) and crediting the asset disposal account, where they are compared with the asset's book value to find the gain or loss. Option C skips the disposal account, and option D reverses the entry.

questions.question: Assume that a vehicle that depreciates on the straight-line basis over 5 years is purchased at a cost of N170,000, and it is expected to have a salvage value of N20,000. Calculate the accumulated depreciation balance at the end of the third year.
questions.explanation: Straight-line depreciation charges the same amount every year: (N170,000 - N20,000) / 5 = N30,000 per year. After three years the accumulated depreciation is N30,000 x 3 = N90,000. Option B is only one year's charge, and option A is the total depreciation over the whole five years.

questions.question: A fixed asset cost $100,000, had a book value of $40,000. It was sold for $10,000. What is the provision for depreciation sold?
questions.explanation: Book value = cost - accumulated depreciation, so the provision for depreciation on the asset sold is $100,000 - $40,000 = $60,000. Option C, $30,000, is the loss on sale ($40,000 - $10,000), not the depreciation.

questions.question: What does it mean by the yearly method of depreciation

options.a: Monthly depreciation in year of purchase and sale
options.b: Full year's depreciation in year of purchase and sale
options.c: Full year's depreciation in year of purchase and no depreciation in year of sale
options.d: No depreciation in the year of purchase and full year's depreciation in year of sale

questions.explanation: Under this method a full year's depreciation is charged in the year an asset is bought, whatever the purchase date, and no depreciation is charged in the year it is sold. Option A describes time-apportioning by months, option B would charge depreciation in both the purchase and sale years, and option D reverses the rule.

questions.question: What type of accounts are Accumulated Depreciation and Allowance for Doubtful Accounts?
questions.explanation: Accumulated depreciation and the allowance (provision) for doubtful debts are contra asset accounts: they carry credit balances that reduce non-current assets and receivables to their carrying amounts. They are not liabilities (Option D), because nothing is owed to anyone, and they are not expenses (Option C), although the yearly depreciation and provision charges are.

questions.question: A machine costs N360,000 and has a useful life span of n years and an expected disposal value of N12,000 with annual depreciation of N69,600. Using the straight-line method of depreciation, what is the useful life of the machine?
questions.explanation: Under straight-line, annual depreciation = (cost - residual value) / useful life, so useful life = (N360,000 - N12,000) / N69,600 = N348,000 / N69,600 = 5 years. Option A (4 years) or C (6 years) would give annual charges of N87,000 and N58,000, which do not match the N69,600 given.

questions.question: What type of entry will increase the balances that are normally found in the accounts Accumulated Depreciation and Allowance for Doubtful Accounts?
questions.explanation: Accumulated depreciation and the allowance for doubtful accounts are contra-asset accounts with normal credit balances, so a credit entry increases them. A debit (A) would reduce them. Options C and D are types of account, not types of entry.

questions.question: A fixed asset cost N100,000. The provision for depreciation brought forward from previous years is N20,000, and the depreciation charge for the current year is N2,000. What net book value will be shown in the balance sheet at the year end?
questions.explanation: Net book value is cost less all depreciation charged to date: N100,000 - (N20,000 brought forward + N2,000 for this year) = N78,000. Option A (N80,000) forgets the current year's charge, and option B (N98,000) deducts only this year's charge and ignores the provision from earlier years.

questions.question: What is ignored in the computation of depreciation of a fixed asset?

options.a: Its estimated residual value at the end of its useful life in the business
options.b: Its length of expected useful economic life to the business

questions.explanation: Depreciation is worked out using the asset's cost, its estimated residual value and its expected useful life (options A, B and C). The cost of repairs is ignored, because ordinary repairs are revenue expenditure charged directly to profit or loss, not part of the depreciable amount.

questions.question: Depreciation is best described as

options.a: Writing off the cost of repairs carried out on an asset
options.b: Spreading the cost of a non-current asset over its useful life
options.c: Recording an increase in the market value of an asset
options.d: Setting aside cash to replace an asset at the end of its life

questions.explanation: Depreciation allocates the cost of a non-current asset, such as a machine or a van, across the years in which it is used. It is not a cash fund for replacement; charging depreciation does not move any money out of the bank.

questions.question: Depreciation can be described as the expired portion of
questions.explanation: Buying a non-current asset is capital expenditure, and the part of that cost used up each year is the depreciation charge. Revenue expenditure, such as rent or wages, is charged in full in the year it is incurred, so there is nothing left to expire later.

questions.question: Charging part of the cost of a delivery van as an expense in each year that the van helps to earn revenue follows the
questions.explanation: Depreciation matches part of the cost of an asset against the revenue it helps to earn in each year of its use. The realisation concept is about when revenue is recognised, not about spreading the cost of an asset over the years.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a method of depreciation?

options.a: Sum of the years' digits method

questions.explanation: The weighted average method is a way of valuing inventory, not of depreciating non-current assets. Straight line, reducing balance and sum of the years' digits are the three depreciation methods named for this course.

questions.question: Which of the following is taken into account when computing the annual depreciation of a machine?
questions.explanation: Depreciation is worked out from the asset's cost, its useful life and its residual value, the amount expected when it is disposed of. Repair costs are ignored, because they are running expenses charged separately, not part of the cost being spread.

questions.question: Under the straight line method, the annual depreciation charge is calculated as

options.a: (Cost - residual value) / useful life in years
options.b: (Cost + residual value) / useful life in years
options.c: (Remaining life / sum of the digits) x cost
options.d: Rate x net book value at the start of the year

questions.explanation: The straight line method spreads the depreciable amount, cost less residual value, equally over the useful life, giving the same charge each year. Rate x net book value at the start of the year is the reducing balance method, which gives a falling charge.

questions.question: Under the reducing balance method, each year's depreciation charge is calculated as

options.a: A fixed rate applied to the original cost every year
options.b: Remaining life over the sum of the digits applied to cost less residual value
options.c: Cost less residual value divided by the useful life
options.d: A fixed rate applied to the net book value at the start of the year

questions.explanation: The reducing balance method applies the same percentage to the net book value at the start of each year, so the charge falls as the book value falls. Applying the rate to the original cost every year would give an equal charge each year, which is how the straight line method behaves.

questions.question: The net book value of a non-current asset is
questions.explanation: Net book value is what remains of the asset's cost after deducting all depreciation charged on it so far. Cost less residual value is the depreciable amount that is spread over the asset's life, not the value at which the asset is carried.

questions.question: A gain made on the disposal of a non-current asset is

options.d: Added directly to the owner's capital account

questions.explanation: A gain on disposal is treated as income for the year, so it is credited to the income statement. Debiting it to the income statement would treat it as a loss and reduce profit, which is the treatment for a loss on disposal.

questions.question: A firm with a 31 December year end bought a machine in March 2023 and sold it in June 2025. Depreciation is N10,000 a year on the straight line method, and the firm uses the yearly method. What total depreciation is charged on the machine over its life in the firm?
questions.explanation: Under the yearly method, a full year is charged in the year of purchase (2023) and in 2024, but nothing in the year of sale (2025), so the total is 2 x 10,000 = N20,000. N30,000 wrongly charges a full year in 2025 as well.

questions.question: For an asset with a useful life of 4 years, the sum of the digits used in the sum of the years' digits method is
questions.explanation: The sum of the years' digits is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10, so the first year's charge is 4/10 of cost less residual value. The figure 4 is just the useful life, not the sum of the digits.

questions.question: A bank in Lagos buys a generator for N2,400,000. It has a useful life of 4 years and a residual value of N400,000. What is the annual depreciation charge using the straight line method?
questions.explanation: Annual charge = (2,400,000 - 400,000) / 4 = N500,000. N600,000 ignores the residual value and divides the full cost by 4.

questions.question: A machine costing N900,000 has a residual value of N100,000 and a useful life of 8 years. Using the straight line method, what is its net book value at the end of year 3?
questions.explanation: The annual charge is (900,000 - 100,000) / 8 = N100,000, so after 3 years accumulated depreciation is N300,000 and NBV = 900,000 - 300,000 = N600,000. N300,000 is the accumulated depreciation, not the net book value.

questions.question: Equipment cost N750,000 and is depreciated by the straight line method over 5 years at N140,000 a year. What residual value was assumed?
questions.explanation: Total depreciation over the life is 140,000 x 5 = N700,000, so residual value = 750,000 - 700,000 = N50,000. N610,000 deducts only one year's charge from the cost.

questions.question: Using a 25% reducing balance rate, what is the second-year depreciation on a delivery van that cost N500,000?
questions.explanation: Year 1 charge is 25% x 500,000 = N125,000, leaving NBV of N375,000, so year 2 charge is 25% x 375,000 = N93,750. N125,000 applies the rate to the original cost again, which is the straight line approach.

questions.question: A printing machine bought by a firm in Ikeja for N800,000 is depreciated at 10% a year on the reducing balance method. What is its net book value at the end of year 3?
questions.explanation: NBV after n years = cost x (1 - rate)^n = 800,000 x 0.9^3 = N583,200. N560,000 deducts 10% of the original cost for each of 3 years, which treats the method as straight line.

questions.question: Office equipment cost N1,000,000. If depreciation is provided at 20% per annum on the reducing balance, how much accumulated depreciation will stand in the books after two years?
questions.explanation: Year 1 charge is N200,000 and year 2 charge is 20% x 800,000 = N160,000, so accumulated depreciation is N360,000. N400,000 charges 20% of cost in both years, which is the straight line result, not reducing balance.

questions.question: Find the year 2 sum-of-the-years'-digits charge for a machine costing N650,000 with a 4-year life and N50,000 residual value.
questions.explanation: The sum of the digits is 10 and the depreciable amount is N600,000; in year 2 the remaining life is 3, so the charge is 3/10 x 600,000 = N180,000. N195,000 applies 3/10 to the full cost and forgets to deduct the residual value.

questions.question: An asset (cost N320,000, residual N20,000, life 5 years) is depreciated on the sum of the years' digits basis. How much is charged in its third year?
questions.explanation: The sum of the digits is 15 and the remaining life at the start of year 3 is 3, so the charge is 3/15 x (320,000 - 20,000) = N60,000. N64,000 applies 3/15 to the full cost without deducting the residual value.

questions.question: A machine cost N600,000, has no residual value and is depreciated by the straight line method over 5 years. It is sold for N300,000 after 3 full years. What is the result on disposal?
questions.explanation: Annual depreciation is N120,000, so after 3 years NBV = 600,000 - 360,000 = N240,000, and selling for N300,000 gives a gain of N60,000. The loss of N300,000 wrongly compares the proceeds with the original cost instead of the net book value.

questions.question: Equipment costing N400,000 is depreciated at 20% a year on the reducing balance method. After 2 full years it is sold for N200,000. What is the result on disposal?
questions.explanation: NBV after 2 years is 400,000 x 0.8^2 = N256,000, and selling for N200,000 gives a loss of N56,000. The loss of N40,000 uses a straight line NBV of N240,000, which does not apply under the reducing balance method.

questions.question: A firm in Ikeja bought a generator for N3,000,000. It has a residual value of N600,000 and a useful life of 6 years. Using the straight line method, what is the accumulated depreciation at the end of year 4?
questions.explanation: The annual charge is (3,000,000 - 600,000) / 6 = N400,000, so after 4 years accumulated depreciation is 4 x 400,000 = N1,600,000. N2,000,000 ignores the residual value, and N1,400,000 is the net book value rather than the accumulated depreciation.

questions.question: What depreciation will be charged in the third year on a N600,000 machine written down at 30% per annum on the reducing balance basis?
questions.explanation: NBV falls to 600,000 x 0.7 = N420,000 after year 1 and to N294,000 after year 2, so year 3 charge is 30% x 294,000 = N88,200. N126,000 is the year 2 charge (30% x 420,000), not the year 3 charge.

questions.question: In the statement of financial position, the net book value of equipment is its cost less the

options.c: Depreciation charge for the current year only
