questions.explanation: The provision for depreciation (accumulated depreciation) holds all depreciation charged on the asset to date, and deducting it from cost gives net book value. Deducting only the current year's charge would ignore depreciation from earlier years and overstate the asset.

questions.question: A machine is depreciated by the straight line method at N90,000 a year over 6 years, and its residual value is N30,000. What did the machine cost?
questions.explanation: Cost less residual value equals total depreciation, 90,000 x 6 = N540,000, so cost = 540,000 + 30,000 = N570,000. N540,000 is only the depreciable amount; it leaves out the residual value that is still part of the cost.

questions.question: Using sum of the years' digits, find the net book value at the end of year 2 of an asset bought for N330,000 (residual value N30,000, useful life 5 years).
questions.explanation: The depreciable amount is N300,000, so year 1 charge is 5/15 x 300,000 = N100,000 and year 2 is 4/15 x 300,000 = N80,000; NBV = 330,000 - 180,000 = N150,000. N210,000 uses straight line depreciation of N60,000 a year instead of the sum of the digits.

questions.question: Which depreciation method gives the same charge in every year of an asset's life?

options.a: Both reducing balance and sum of the years' digits
options.b: Sum of the years' digits method

questions.explanation: The straight line method divides cost less residual value equally by the useful life, so the charge is the same every year. The reducing balance method gives a falling charge because the rate is applied to a falling net book value.

questions.question: What is the first-year charge on a N440,000 machine (residual value N20,000, 6-year life) under the sum of the years' digits method?
questions.explanation: The sum of the digits for 6 years is 21, so year 1 charge is 6/21 x (440,000 - 20,000) = N120,000. N125,714 applies 6/21 to the full cost without deducting the residual value.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: The trial balance of Olumide Bakare & Co shows a Trade receivable balance of N2,500,000 as at 31 December, 2012 while the provision for doubtful debt was given as N500,000.00. Additional information was given to the effect that the provision for doubtful debt should be N750,000.00 of trade receivables. How much should reflect in Profit and Loss account as cost?
questions.explanation: Only the increase in the provision is charged to profit and loss: N750,000 - N500,000 = N250,000. Option C is the full new provision, which would double-count the N500,000 already charged in earlier years.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: Trial Balance of a business shows a trade receivables balance of N30,000. Allowance for doubtful debt is to be 5% of total trade receivables, while allowance for discount on trade receivables is to be 2% of the trade receivables remaining after deducting the allowance for doubtful debt. The amount to show on the Statement of financial position as net Trade receivables is
questions.explanation: First deduct the allowance for doubtful debts: 5% x N30,000 = N1,500, leaving N28,500. The discount allowance is then 2% x N28,500 = N570, so net trade receivables = N30,000 - N1,500 - N570 = N27,930. Option A (N27,900) takes the 2% on the full N30,000, and options C and D are allowance totals, not net receivables.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: Olude Enterprises had bad debts of N3,000 and accumulated provision for bad debts of N3,500. It is desired to make the provision of N4,000 at the end of the year. The total amount to be debited to P & L A/C is:
questions.explanation: The charge to profit or loss is the bad debts written off plus the increase in the provision: N3,000 + (N4,000 - N3,500) = N3,500. Option A (N4,000) is just the new provision, and option C (N6,500) adds the bad debts to the old provision instead of charging only the increase.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: At the end of the financial year, accounts receivables have a balance of N100,000 and provision for the bad & doubtful debts provided amounting to N70,000. The Net realizable value of the accounts receivable in the statement of financial position is:
questions.explanation: Receivables are shown net of the provision for bad and doubtful debts: N100,000 - N70,000 = N30,000. Option A (N170,000) adds the provision instead of deducting it, and option D (N100,000) ignores the provision altogether.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: A customer owing N40,000 to a trader in Balogun market is declared bankrupt, and the debt is written off. The correct entry is

options.a: Debit cash, credit the customer's account
options.c: Debit bad debts, credit the customer's account
options.d: Debit the customer's account, credit bad debts

questions.explanation: Writing off a bad debt charges an expense (debit bad debts) and removes the amount from the customer's receivable balance (credit the customer). Debiting cash is wrong because no money has been received from the bankrupt customer.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: What effect does writing off a bad debt have on the statement of financial position?

options.b: It increases the provision for depreciation

questions.explanation: The customer's account is credited when the debt is written off, so the amount owed to the business, trade receivables, goes down. Trade payables are amounts the business owes its suppliers, so they are not affected.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: In the income statement, bad debts written off are treated as
questions.explanation: A bad debt is a loss to the business, so it is debited to the bad debts account and charged as an expense, reducing profit. Treating it as a current asset is wrong, because the amount can no longer be collected and has been removed from receivables.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: A provision for doubtful debts is

options.a: Discounts given to customers for paying promptly
options.b: An estimate of debts that may not be collected
options.c: Debts that have already been written off as irrecoverable
options.d: The total amount owed by all credit customers

questions.explanation: A provision for doubtful debts is an estimate of the part of receivables that may not be collected, made before any particular debt has gone bad. Debts already written off are bad debts, which are actual losses, not an estimate.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: In the statement of financial position, the provision for doubtful debts is shown

options.b: As an addition to trade receivables
options.c: As a deduction from trade receivables

questions.explanation: The provision reduces trade receivables to the amount the business expects to collect, so it is deducted from receivables. It is not a liability, because the business does not owe anyone this amount.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: Making a provision for doubtful debts, so that receivables are not shown at more than the amount expected to be collected, follows the
questions.explanation: Prudence requires that assets are not overstated, so the business provides for debts that may not be collected. The going concern concept assumes the business will continue operating, which does not deal with the risk of customers not paying.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: When a provision for doubtful debts already exists from the previous year, the amount taken to profit or loss in respect of the provision this year is

options.b: The full new provision plus the old provision
options.c: Only the change (increase or decrease) in the provision

questions.explanation: The old provision has already been charged in earlier years, so only the change in the provision is taken to profit or loss. Charging the full new provision would count the old part twice.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: A reduction in the provision for doubtful debts is treated in the income statement as
questions.explanation: When the provision falls, part of an amount charged in earlier years is no longer needed, so the decrease is credited to profit or loss as income. Treating it as an expense is the rule for an increase in the provision, not a decrease.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: The double entry to record an increase in the provision for doubtful debts is

options.a: Debit profit and loss account, credit provision for doubtful debts
options.b: Debit provision for doubtful debts, credit trade receivables
options.c: Debit trade receivables, credit provision for doubtful debts
options.d: Debit provision for doubtful debts, credit profit and loss account

questions.explanation: An increase in the provision is an expense, so profit and loss is debited, and the provision, a contra-asset account, is increased by a credit. Debiting the provision and crediting profit and loss is the entry for a decrease in the provision.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: When the provision for doubtful debts is reduced at the year end, which entry records the reduction?

options.a: Debit profit and loss account, credit provision for doubtful debts
options.b: Debit trade receivables, credit profit and loss account
options.c: Debit provision for doubtful debts, credit profit and loss account
options.d: Debit bad debts, credit trade receivables

questions.explanation: A decrease reduces the provision, a contra-asset normally increased by credits, so the provision is debited and profit and loss is credited with the income. Debiting profit and loss and crediting the provision is the entry for an increase, which would be an expense.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: A provision for discount on debtors is calculated on

options.a: Total trade receivables before any provision is deducted
options.b: The provision for doubtful debts itself
options.c: Trade payables at the year end
options.d: Trade receivables remaining after deducting the provision for doubtful debts

questions.explanation: Discount is only expected to be given to customers who will actually pay, so it is worked out on receivables after deducting the provision for doubtful debts. Calculating it on total receivables before the doubtful debt provision would allow a discount on debts that may never be collected.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: In the profit and loss account, an increase in the provision for bad debts appears as
questions.explanation: An increase in the provision for bad debts reduces profit, so it is debited to profit and loss as an expense. A credit as income would be the treatment of a decrease in the provision.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: A trader fails to write off a debt of N15,000 that is known to be irrecoverable. What is the effect on the accounts?

options.a: Profit is overstated and trade receivables understated by N15,000
options.b: Profit is understated and trade receivables overstated by N15,000
options.c: Profit and trade receivables are both understated by N15,000
options.d: Profit and trade receivables are both overstated by N15,000

questions.explanation: The missing write-off means the bad debts expense of N15,000 is left out, so profit is too high, and the uncollectable debt is still counted in receivables, so they are too high as well. Profit cannot be understated, because a missing expense always makes profit look bigger.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: A business in Ikeja had a provision for doubtful debts of N40,000 at the start of the year. At the year end the provision is to be N55,000. What amount is charged to profit and loss for the provision?
questions.explanation: Only the change goes to profit and loss: 55,000 - 40,000 = N15,000, charged as an expense. N55,000 charges the whole new provision, but N40,000 of it was already charged in earlier years.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: A firm's provision for doubtful debts is to be reduced from N80,000 to N65,000 at the year end. How is this treated in profit and loss?
questions.explanation: The provision falls by 80,000 - 65,000 = N15,000, and a decrease in the provision is income, so N15,000 is credited to profit and loss. Debiting N15,000 as an expense treats the change as an increase, which it is not.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: Trade receivables at the year end are N600,000, and the provision for doubtful debts is to be 5% of receivables. The provision brought forward from last year is N20,000. What is charged to profit and loss for the provision this year?
questions.explanation: The required provision is 5% x 600,000 = N30,000, so the increase is 30,000 - 20,000 = N10,000. N30,000 charges the whole required provision instead of just the increase.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: Trade receivables before adjustments are N820,000. A debt of N20,000 is to be written off, and the provision for doubtful debts is to be 5% of the remaining receivables. The existing provision is N25,000. What is the total charge to profit and loss for bad and doubtful debts?
questions.explanation: Remaining receivables are N800,000, so the provision should be N40,000, an increase of N15,000; the total charge is 20,000 + 15,000 = N35,000. N36,000 calculates the 5% on N820,000 before the write-off, which overstates the provision.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: Trade receivables are N950,000 before a bad debt of N50,000 is written off. The provision for doubtful debts is to be 10% of the remaining receivables. What figure is shown for net trade receivables in the statement of financial position?
questions.explanation: After the write-off, receivables are N900,000 and the provision is 10% x 900,000 = N90,000, so net receivables are 900,000 - 90,000 = N810,000. N805,000 takes 10% of N950,000 before the write-off, which overstates the provision.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: During the year, a business wrote off bad debts of N6,000. Its provision for doubtful debts was reduced from N12,000 to N9,000. What is the net charge to profit and loss for bad and doubtful debts?
questions.explanation: The bad debts of N6,000 are an expense, while the N3,000 fall in the provision is income, so the net charge is 6,000 - 3,000 = N3,000. N9,000 adds the decrease instead of deducting it, treating it as an expense.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: A trader in Balogun market creates a provision for doubtful debts for the first time, at 3% of trade receivables of N300,000. What is charged to profit and loss for the provision this year?

options.c: Nil, since there was no previous provision

questions.explanation: With no opening provision, the whole new provision of 3% x 300,000 = N9,000 is the increase and is charged to profit and loss. Saying nil is wrong, because moving from no provision to N9,000 is itself an increase of N9,000.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: Trade receivables are N200,000. The provision for doubtful debts is 5% of receivables, and the provision for discount on debtors is 2.5% of receivables after the doubtful debt provision. What is the provision for discount on debtors?
questions.explanation: The doubtful debt provision is N10,000, leaving N190,000, so the discount provision is 2.5% x 190,000 = N4,750. N5,000 applies 2.5% to the full N200,000, ignoring that discount is worked out after the doubtful debt provision.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: A Lagos wholesaler has trade receivables of N400,000. It makes a provision for doubtful debts of 10%, and then a provision for discount of 5% on the receivables remaining after the doubtful debt provision. What is the net trade receivables figure in the statement of financial position?
questions.explanation: The doubtful debt provision is N40,000, leaving N360,000; the discount provision is 5% x 360,000 = N18,000, so net receivables are N342,000. N340,000 works out the 5% discount on the full N400,000 instead of on the reduced figure.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: A business had a provision for doubtful debts of N10,000 at the start of the year. During the year bad debts of N4,000 were written off, and the total charge to profit and loss for bad and doubtful debts was N9,000. What is the provision at the end of the year?
questions.explanation: Of the N9,000 charge, N4,000 is bad debts, so the increase in provision is N5,000, and the closing provision is 10,000 + 5,000 = N15,000. N5,000 is only the increase, not the closing balance of the provision.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: A firm's provision for doubtful debts of N12,500 is 5% of its trade receivables. What is the amount of trade receivables?
questions.explanation: If 5% of receivables is N12,500, then receivables are 12,500 / 0.05 = N250,000. N237,500 is the net receivables after deducting the provision, not the receivables on which the 5% was worked out.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: A trader's draft net profit is N500,000. He has not yet written off bad debts of N20,000 or increased the provision for doubtful debts by N8,000. What is the corrected net profit?
questions.explanation: Both the bad debts and the increase in provision are expenses, so profit falls to 500,000 - 20,000 - 8,000 = N472,000. N480,000 deducts the bad debts but forgets the increase in the provision.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: The draft net profit of a firm in Ikeja is N300,000 before adjusting for a decrease of N5,000 in the provision for doubtful debts. There are no bad debts this year. What is the corrected net profit?
questions.explanation: A decrease in the provision is income, so it is added to profit: 300,000 + 5,000 = N305,000. N295,000 deducts the decrease as though it were an expense.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: During the year, a business wrote off bad debts of N2,000, and its provision for doubtful debts fell by N5,000. What is the net effect on profit and loss?
questions.explanation: The bad debts are an N2,000 expense and the N5,000 fall in the provision is income, giving a net credit of 5,000 - 2,000 = N3,000. A net debit of N7,000 wrongly treats the decrease in the provision as an expense and adds it to the bad debts.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: A firm keeps its provision for doubtful debts at 5% of trade receivables. Receivables were N400,000 last year and are N360,000 this year. How is the change in the provision treated this year?

options.a: N18,000 debited to profit and loss as an expense
options.b: N2,000 debited to profit and loss as an expense
options.c: N38,000 debited to profit and loss as an expense
options.d: N2,000 credited to profit and loss as income

questions.explanation: Last year's provision was N20,000 and this year's is 5% x 360,000 = N18,000, a decrease of N2,000, which is credited to profit and loss as income. Debiting N18,000 charges the whole new provision instead of only the change.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: A business has trade receivables of N15,000 before writing off bad debts of N1,000. It then creates, for the first time, a provision for doubtful debts of 10% of the remaining receivables. What is the total charge to profit and loss for bad and doubtful debts?
questions.explanation: Remaining receivables are N14,000, so the provision is N1,400, and the total charge is 1,000 + 1,400 = N2,400. N2,500 takes 10% of N15,000 before the write-off, which overstates the provision.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: Another name for the provision for doubtful debts is the
questions.explanation: The provision for doubtful debts is also called the allowance for doubtful debts; both describe the estimate deducted from receivables. Bad debts written off are actual losses already removed from receivables, so they are a different item.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: The main difference between a bad debt and a provision for doubtful debts is that

options.a: A bad debt is written off as uncollectable, while a provision is an estimate of debts that may not be collected
options.b: A bad debt is added to receivables, while a provision is added to payables
options.c: A provision is written off as uncollectable, while a bad debt is an estimate of debts that may not be collected
options.d: A bad debt is shown as a current liability, while a provision is shown as a current asset

questions.explanation: A bad debt is a specific debt removed from the books because it will not be paid, while a provision is only an estimate of debts that may not be collected. The option that swaps the two descriptions reverses the meaning of both terms.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the provision for doubtful debts is NOT correct?

options.a: The full balance of the provision is charged to profit and loss every year
options.c: A decrease in it is treated as income
options.d: It is shown as a deduction from trade receivables

questions.explanation: Only the change in the provision is taken to profit and loss each year, not the full balance. The statement that a decrease is treated as income is correct, since a lower provision releases part of an earlier charge back to profit.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: Trade receivables are N80,000 before writing off a bad debt of N5,000. A provision for doubtful debts of 4% of the remaining receivables is then made. What figure is shown for net trade receivables?
questions.explanation: After the write-off, receivables are N75,000, and the provision is 4% x 75,000 = N3,000, so net receivables are N72,000. N71,800 works out the 4% on the N80,000 before the write-off, giving a provision that is too large.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: An increase of N12,000 in the provision for doubtful debts has which effect on the accounts?

options.a: It reduces net trade receivables but does not affect net profit
options.b: It reduces both net profit and net trade receivables by N12,000
options.c: It reduces net profit but does not affect net trade receivables
options.d: It increases net profit and reduces net trade receivables

questions.explanation: The increase is charged to profit and loss as an expense, lowering net profit, and the larger provision is deducted from receivables, lowering net receivables, both by N12,000. Saying profit is unaffected ignores that an increase in the provision is an expense.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: Bayo, a wholesaler in Ikeja, expects that about 5% of his customers' balances may never be paid, although no customer has yet defaulted. What should he do at the year end?

options.a: Record a 5% liability to his customers
options.b: Write off 5% of trade receivables as bad debts
options.d: Create a provision for doubtful debts

questions.explanation: Because no specific debt has gone bad, Bayo should make a provision for doubtful debts, which is an estimate of debts that may not be collected. Writing off 5% as bad debts would be wrong, since bad debts are written off only when particular debts are known to be uncollectable.

questions.topic: Bad debts and doubtful debt provisions
questions.question: A Lagos distributor's trade receivables were N500,000 at both the start and the end of the year, but the provision for doubtful debts was raised from 2% to 4% of receivables. What is charged to profit and loss for the provision this year?

options.b: Nil, since receivables did not change

questions.explanation: The provision rises from 2% x 500,000 = N10,000 to 4% x 500,000 = N20,000, so the increase of N10,000 is charged as an expense. N20,000 is the whole new provision, but only the change in the provision goes to profit and loss.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: Which one of the following is not a reporting category in the income statement?
questions.explanation: An income statement is presented under headings such as revenue, cost of sales, distribution costs and operating profit or loss. The trading account is a bookkeeping account used to work out gross profit, not a reporting category of the statement itself. Options A, B and D are all standard headings.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: The financial statement that reports the portion of change in owner's equity resulting from revenues and expenses during a specified time interval is the
questions.explanation: The profit and loss account (income statement) shows revenues minus expenses for a period, which is exactly the part of the change in owner's equity caused by trading. A journal (Option A) is a book of entry, a liability (Option B) is an obligation, and dividends (Option D) are distributions to owners, not a statement.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: The financial statement with a structure that is similar to the accounting equation is the
questions.explanation: The balance sheet lists assets on one side and liabilities plus owner's equity on the other, which follows the accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Equity. A trial balance (Option D) also balances, but it lists debits and credits for all accounts, including income and expenses, so it does not follow the equation's structure.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: Financial statements are reports that allow interested parties to evaluate the profitability and solvency of a business. This statement do not includes one of the following
questions.explanation: The main financial statements are the income statement (profit or loss), the statement of owner's equity (changes in equity) and the balance sheet (statement of financial position), so an "expenditure statement" is not one of them. Options A, C and D are all standard financial statements used to judge profitability and solvency.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: A balance sheet is drawn up to ascertain

options.a: The assets owned by the reporting entity as at the balance sheet date
options.b: The liabilities owed by the reporting as at the balance sheet date
options.c: The profit/loss made by the reporting entity for the period to the balance sheet date
options.d: The financial position of the reporting entity as at the balance sheet date

questions.explanation: A balance sheet shows the financial position of the business at a particular date by listing its assets, liabilities and capital together. Options A and B describe only one part of the balance sheet. Option C describes the profit and loss account, which covers a period rather than a single date.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: A trader's inventory was N1,000 higher at the end of a year than at the beginning of the year. Net sales for the year were N25,000 and purchases were N14,000. As a result, the year's

options.a: cost of goods sold was N15,000
options.c: gross profit was 48% of net sales.
options.d: cost of goods available for sales was N13,000

questions.explanation: Closing inventory is N1,000 higher than opening, so cost of goods sold = purchases - increase in inventory = N14,000 - N1,000 = N13,000. Gross profit = N25,000 - N13,000 = N12,000, which is N12,000 / N25,000 = 48% of net sales. Option A (N15,000) adds the inventory increase instead of subtracting it, and option B (N14,000) confuses gross profit with purchases.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: A trader has the following data pertaining to the year ended 31st December 20X2: Opening Inventory N340,000, Purchases N900,000, Closing Inventory N420,000, Carriage Inwards N100,000, Carriage Outwards N150,000. The cost of goods sold during the year was
questions.explanation: Cost of goods sold = opening inventory + purchases + carriage inwards - closing inventory = N340,000 + N900,000 + N100,000 - N420,000 = N920,000. Carriage outwards is a selling expense in the profit or loss, not part of cost of goods sold, so option C (N970,000), which uses carriage outwards instead of carriage inwards, is wrong. Option A (N770,000) wrongly deducts carriage outwards.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: The following information is extracted from the records of a trading entity for the year ended 31st December 20X2: Opening inventory N990,000, Purchases N3,740,000, Carriage inwards N22,000, Sales N5,280,000. The gross profit recorded was 25% of sales. What was the closing inventory as at 31st December 20X2?
questions.explanation: Gross profit is 25% of sales, so cost of sales = 75% x N5,280,000 = N3,960,000. Closing inventory = opening inventory + purchases + carriage inwards - cost of sales = N990,000 + N3,740,000 + N22,000 - N3,960,000 = N792,000. Option A (N770,000) forgets the carriage inwards, and option D (N1,320,000) is simply the gross profit figure.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: All of the following are contra (or reduction) accounts except
questions.explanation: A contra account reduces another account: accumulated depreciation (A) and provision for doubtful debts (B) reduce assets, while sales returns (C) reduce sales. Carriage inwards is not a reduction of anything; it is an extra cost added to purchases in the trading account, which makes it the exception.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: Which of the following results in over-stated gross profit?
questions.explanation: Closing stock is deducted in working out cost of goods sold, so if it is overstated, cost of goods sold is too low and gross profit is too high. Overstating purchases, carriage inwards or opening stock (options A, C and D) increases cost of goods sold and so understates gross profit.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: If sales are N8200, opening stock N1300, closing stock N900, purchases N6400, carriage inwards N200, the cost of goods sold figure is
questions.explanation: Cost of goods sold = opening stock + purchases + carriage inwards - closing stock = N1,300 + N6,400 + N200 - N900 = N7,000. Sales do not enter this calculation. Option C (N6,800) forgets to add the carriage inwards.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: Calculate the gross profit if rate of gross profit is 20% on sales and cost of goods is N120,000
questions.explanation: If gross profit is 20% of sales, cost of goods is 80% of sales, so sales = N120,000 / 0.8 = N150,000 and gross profit = 20% x N150,000 = N30,000. Option A (N24,000) wrongly takes 20% of the cost instead of the sales.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: Opening stock N8,500; Purchases N30,700; Wages N4,800; Return inwards N5,200; Closing Stock N9,000. Cost of goods sold will be:
questions.explanation: Cost of goods sold = opening stock N8,500 + purchases N30,700 + wages N4,800 - closing stock N9,000 = N35,000, with wages treated as a direct cost of getting the goods ready for sale. Return inwards is deducted from sales, not from cost of goods sold, so option A (N29,800), which subtracts it, is wrong.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: A firm purchased goods of N90,000 and spent N6,000 on freight towards it. At the end of the year the cost of goods still unsold was N12,000. Sales during the year N120,000. What is the gross profit earned by the firm?
questions.explanation: Cost of goods sold = purchases + freight (carriage inwards) - unsold goods = N90,000 + N6,000 - N12,000 = N84,000. Gross profit = N120,000 - N84,000 = N36,000. Option C (N42,000) ignores the freight, which is part of the cost of the goods.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: A person started a business with capital of N50,000 and he takes loan from his relative N5,000. Profit for the year is N10,000 and drawings N9,000. What will be the amount of closing capital?
questions.explanation: Closing capital = opening capital + profit - drawings = N50,000 + N10,000 - N9,000 = N51,000. The loan from the relative is a liability, not capital, so option C (N56,000), which adds it, is wrong. Option A (N60,000) forgets to deduct drawings.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: Sales = N300,000; G.P. on sales is 20%; Purchases = N240,000; opening stock = N20,000. Find closing stock
questions.explanation: Gross profit is 20% of sales, so cost of goods sold = 80% x N300,000 = N240,000. Closing stock = opening stock + purchases - cost of goods sold = N20,000 + N240,000 - N240,000 = N20,000. Closing stock equals opening stock here because purchases exactly match cost of goods sold, so options B, C and D cannot be right.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: The fixed assets of a company is double of the current assets and half of capital. If the current assets are N300,000 and investments N400,000. Calculate the current liabilities assuming that there are no other items in the balance sheet
questions.explanation: Fixed assets are double current assets: 2 x N300,000 = N600,000, and capital is double fixed assets: 2 x N600,000 = N1,200,000. Total assets = N600,000 + N300,000 + N400,000 = N1,300,000, so current liabilities = N1,300,000 - N1,200,000 = N100,000. Option C (N1,300,000) is total assets, and option A (N1,200,000) is capital.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: A trader in Balogun market made sales of N900,000 during the year, and customers returned goods worth N40,000. What is the net sales figure in the trading account?
questions.explanation: Net sales = sales - returns inwards = 900,000 - 40,000 = N860,000. N940,000 adds the returns instead of deducting them, but goods sent back by customers reduce sales.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: A business has: opening inventory N120,000; purchases N600,000; carriage inwards N15,000; returns outwards N25,000; closing inventory N90,000. What is the cost of goods sold?
questions.explanation: Cost of goods sold = 120,000 + 600,000 + 15,000 - 25,000 - 90,000 = N620,000. N670,000 adds returns outwards instead of deducting them, but goods returned to suppliers reduce purchases.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: For the year ended 31 December 2025, a sole trader had: sales N1,000,000; returns inwards N30,000; opening inventory N150,000; purchases N700,000; carriage inwards N20,000; returns outwards N10,000; closing inventory N180,000. What is the gross profit?
questions.explanation: Net sales are 1,000,000 - 30,000 = N970,000, and cost of goods sold is 150,000 + 700,000 + 20,000 - 10,000 - 180,000 = N680,000, so gross profit is N290,000. N320,000 ignores the returns inwards, which must be deducted from sales.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: In the final accounts of a sole trader, carriage outwards is shown

options.a: As a current asset in the statement of financial position
options.b: As a selling and distribution expense in the profit and loss account
options.c: As part of the cost of goods sold in the trading account
options.d: As a deduction from sales in the trading account

questions.explanation: Carriage outwards is the cost of delivering goods to customers, so it is a selling and distribution expense in the profit and loss account. It is not part of cost of goods sold; that treatment applies to carriage inwards, the cost of bringing goods in.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: Where is carriage inwards treated when a sole trader prepares final accounts?

options.a: Deducted from purchases in the trading account
options.b: Shown as a selling and distribution expense in the profit and loss account
options.c: Deducted from sales in the trading account
options.d: Added in arriving at cost of goods sold in the trading account

questions.explanation: Carriage inwards is part of the cost of getting goods into the business, so it is added in calculating cost of goods sold. Treating it as a selling and distribution expense confuses it with carriage outwards, which is the cost of delivering goods to customers.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: In the trading account, returns inwards are

options.a: Added in arriving at cost of goods sold
options.c: Shown as an expense in the profit and loss account
options.d: Deducted from sales to give net sales

questions.explanation: Returns inwards are goods sent back by customers, so they reduce sales and are deducted to arrive at net sales. Deducting them from purchases confuses them with returns outwards, which are goods the business sends back to its suppliers.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: In calculating cost of goods sold, returns outwards are
questions.explanation: Returns outwards are goods the business sends back to its suppliers, so they reduce purchases in the cost of goods sold calculation. Deducting them from sales confuses them with returns inwards, which are goods returned by customers.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: A sole trader's gross profit is N400,000, and he also received rent of N10,000. Expenses were: rent paid N80,000; salaries N120,000; depreciation N30,000; increase in provision for doubtful debts N5,000. What is the net profit?
questions.explanation: Net profit = gross profit + other income - expenses = 400,000 + 10,000 - (80,000 + 120,000 + 30,000 + 5,000) = N175,000. N155,000 deducts the rent received as though it were an expense instead of adding it as income.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: A trader's opening capital was N800,000. Net profit for the year was N175,000 and drawings were N60,000. What is the closing capital?
questions.explanation: Closing capital = opening capital + net profit - drawings = 800,000 + 175,000 - 60,000 = N915,000. N1,035,000 adds the drawings, but drawings take value out of the business and reduce capital.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: Which of the following is a current asset in the statement of financial position of a sole trader?
questions.explanation: Prepayments are amounts paid in advance for benefits still to be received, so they are current assets. A bank overdraft, accrued expenses and income received in advance are all amounts the business owes, so they are current liabilities.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: In the statement of financial position, non-current assets are shown at
questions.explanation: Non-current assets are shown at net book value, that is, cost less accumulated depreciation. Showing them at original cost with no deduction would ignore the depreciation already charged and overstate the assets.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: The income statement of a sole trader is made up of

options.a: The profit and loss account and the cash book
options.b: The trading account and the profit and loss account
options.c: The statement of financial position and the trial balance
options.d: The trading account and the statement of financial position

questions.explanation: The income statement combines the trading account, which works out gross profit, and the profit and loss account, which works out net profit. The statement of financial position is a separate statement showing the position as at a date, not part of the income statement.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: A sole trader's capital was N500,000 at the start of the year and N620,000 at the end. Net profit for the year was N200,000. What were the drawings for the year?
questions.explanation: Closing capital = opening capital + net profit - drawings, so 620,000 = 500,000 + 200,000 - drawings, giving drawings of N80,000. N120,000 is just the increase in capital, which ignores the profit added during the year.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: Opening capital of a trader in Ikeja was N300,000, drawings were N50,000 and closing capital was N400,000. What was the net profit for the year?
questions.explanation: From closing capital = opening capital + net profit - drawings, 400,000 = 300,000 + net profit - 50,000, so net profit is N150,000. N100,000 is only the increase in capital and forgets that drawings of N50,000 were also taken out.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: If the closing inventory of a business is understated, what is the effect on the trading account for the year?

options.b: Cost of goods sold is understated

questions.explanation: Closing inventory is deducted in arriving at cost of goods sold, so a figure that is too low makes cost of goods sold too high and gross profit too low. Gross profit would be overstated only if closing inventory were overstated, the opposite case.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: A business made sales of N600,000, and its gross profit was 25% of sales. What was the cost of goods sold?
questions.explanation: Gross profit is 25% x 600,000 = N150,000, so cost of goods sold = 600,000 - 150,000 = N450,000. N480,000 treats the 25% as a mark-up on cost (600,000 / 1.25), but the question gives the percentage on sales.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: In the final accounts of a sole trader, depreciation of motor vehicles for the year is shown

options.a: As an expense in the profit and loss account
options.c: As part of cost of goods sold in the trading account
options.d: As an addition to gross profit

questions.explanation: Depreciation is one of the expenses deducted from gross profit in the profit and loss account to arrive at net profit. It is not part of cost of goods sold, which covers only the cost of the goods sold such as inventory, purchases and carriage inwards.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: A sole trader took a bank loan repayable in 5 years' time. In the statement of financial position at the year end, the loan is shown as
questions.explanation: A loan that is not repayable for several years is a non-current liability. It is not part of capital, because it is owed to the bank, not to the owner.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: In the profit and loss account, net profit is arrived at by

options.a: Adding drawings to gross profit and deducting expenses
options.b: Deducting closing capital from opening capital
options.c: Adding other income to gross profit and deducting expenses
options.d: Deducting cost of goods sold from net sales

questions.explanation: The profit and loss account starts with gross profit, adds other income and deducts expenses such as depreciation and bad debts to give net profit. Deducting cost of goods sold from net sales gives gross profit, which is the trading account step, not net profit.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: A sole trader's statement of financial position shows total assets of N2,000,000, current liabilities of N300,000 and a long-term bank loan of N500,000. What is the owner's capital?
questions.explanation: The statement of financial position mirrors the accounting equation, so capital = assets - liabilities = 2,000,000 - 300,000 - 500,000 = N1,200,000. N1,700,000 deducts only the current liabilities and forgets that the long-term loan is also a liability.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: A trader's cost of goods sold was N500,000. Opening inventory was N80,000 and closing inventory was N100,000. What were the purchases for the year?
questions.explanation: Cost of goods sold = opening inventory + purchases - closing inventory, so 500,000 = 80,000 + purchases - 100,000, giving purchases of N520,000. N480,000 comes from adding closing inventory and deducting opening inventory, which reverses the formula.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: A firm in Ikeja had: sales N2,500,000; returns inwards N100,000; opening inventory N300,000; purchases N1,600,000; carriage outwards N50,000; closing inventory N400,000. What is the gross profit?
questions.explanation: Net sales are N2,400,000 and cost of goods sold is 300,000 + 1,600,000 - 400,000 = N1,500,000, so gross profit is N900,000. N850,000 wrongly includes carriage outwards in cost of goods sold, but it is a selling expense in the profit and loss account.

questions.topic: Final accounts of a sole trader
questions.question: In the statement of financial position of a sole trader, the net profit for the year is
questions.explanation: Net profit belongs to the owner, so it is added to opening capital, and drawings are then deducted to give closing capital. Adding it to drawings is wrong, because drawings are value the owner takes out, which reduces capital.

questions.question: Which of the following is not an attribute of financial accounting?

options.b: It does not record financial transactions
options.c: It reports financial information about a business entity
options.d: It treats business as a separate entity

questions.explanation: Financial accounting does record financial transactions, so the statement that it does not is false and is therefore not an attribute. Options A, C and D are true: financial accounting looks at past events, reports on a business entity, and treats the business as separate from its owner.

questions.question: Which branch of accounting provides managers with information for internal planning, control and decision-making?
questions.explanation: Management accounting serves people inside the business, giving managers information they need to plan, control operations and make decisions. Financial accounting is the tempting choice, but its reports are historical and prepared mainly for external users such as shareholders and lenders.

questions.question: The branch of accounting that is concerned mainly with ascertaining product and process costs is
questions.explanation: Cost accounting works out what it costs to make each product or run each process. Financial accounting reports the results of the whole business to outsiders and does not give the cost of individual products, which is exactly the gap cost accounting fills.

questions.question: An independent examination of the financial statements of an organisation is known as
questions.explanation: Auditing is the independent examination of financial statements that have already been prepared. Bookkeeping may look close, but it is only the recording of transactions as they happen, not an independent check on the finished statements.

questions.question: Which branch of accounting deals with tax computation and tax planning?
questions.explanation: Taxation is the branch that computes the tax a person or business owes and plans its tax affairs. Financial management also deals with money decisions, but its focus is on raising and using funds, not on working out tax.

questions.question: The raising and use of funds in a business is the main concern of which branch of accounting?
questions.explanation: Financial management deals with how a business raises funds and how it uses them. Financial accounting sounds similar, but it records transactions and produces historical reports for external users rather than deciding how money is raised and used.

questions.question: Which branch of accounting produces historical reports mainly for external users such as shareholders and lenders?
questions.explanation: Financial accounting records past transactions and summarises them in financial statements for outsiders like shareholders and lenders. Management accounting is the tempting option, but it is aimed at managers inside the business for planning, control and decisions.

questions.question: Management accounting is best described as

options.a: The computation of tax payable and tax planning
options.b: The preparation of historical reports for external users
options.c: The provision of information for internal planning, control and decisions
options.d: An independent examination of the financial statements

questions.explanation: Management accounting gives managers inside the organisation the information they need to plan, control and decide. Preparing historical reports for external users describes financial accounting, which looks back and faces outward rather than inward.

questions.question: Auditing is best described as

options.a: The determination of product and process costs
options.b: The raising and use of funds in a business
options.c: An independent examination of the financial statements
options.d: The day-to-day recording of transactions in the books

questions.explanation: Auditing means an independent check of financial statements that the business has already prepared. Day-to-day recording of transactions is bookkeeping, which produces the records that an auditor later examines.

questions.question: Financial management, as a branch of accounting, is concerned mainly with

options.a: Raising funds and deciding how they are used
options.c: Recording transactions for reports to outsiders
options.d: Ascertaining the cost of each product made

questions.explanation: Financial management focuses on where a business gets its funds and how it puts them to use. Recording transactions for reports to outsiders is the work of financial accounting, which is easy to confuse with financial management because the names are similar.

questions.question: Cost accounting is concerned mainly with

options.a: Computing tax payable and tax planning
options.b: Preparing historical reports for external users

questions.explanation: Cost accounting finds out how much each product or process costs, which helps with pricing and cost control. Preparing historical reports for external users describes financial accounting, which reports on the whole business and not on the cost of individual products.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a specialised branch of accounting?
questions.explanation: Marketing research belongs to marketing, not accounting, so it is not a branch of accounting. Auditing, taxation and cost accounting are all specialised branches, together with financial management and management accounting.

questions.question: Financial management, cost accounting, management accounting, taxation and ______ are the specialised branches of accounting commonly named alongside financial accounting.
questions.explanation: Auditing completes the list of five specialised branches: financial management, cost accounting, management accounting, taxation and auditing. Banking and insurance are industries that use accounting, but they are not branches of accounting themselves.

questions.question: A plastic-chair manufacturer in Ikeja wants to know exactly how much it costs to produce one chair. Which branch of accounting will provide this information?
questions.explanation: Working out the cost of each unit produced is the core job of cost accounting, which deals with product and process costs. Financial management may sound relevant because money is involved, but it is about raising and using funds, not costing a product.

questions.question: A bank in Lagos engages an independent firm of accountants to examine the financial statements it has prepared for the year. This work falls under which branch of accounting?
questions.explanation: An independent examination of financial statements already prepared is auditing. Management accounting is done for the bank's own managers to plan and control, and it is not an independent examination of the statements.

questions.question: A trader in Balogun market hires an accountant to work out how much tax he owes on his profit and to plan his tax affairs for next year. This is an example of which branch of accounting?
questions.explanation: Computing tax payable and planning tax affairs is the work of the taxation branch. Auditing involves money records too, but it is an independent examination of financial statements, not a computation of tax.

questions.question: A firm in Ikeja is deciding whether to raise money for expansion through a bank loan or through extra capital from its owners, and how best to use the money. Which branch of accounting is most concerned with this?
questions.explanation: Choosing how to raise funds and how to use them is the focus of financial management. Financial accounting is tempting because of the name, but it records past transactions and reports historical results rather than deciding how to raise and use funds.

questions.question: The managing director of a company in Ikeja wants monthly reports comparing actual results with the budget so that she can control operations. Which branch of accounting provides such reports?
questions.explanation: Comparing actual results with budget for control is internal information for managers, which is what management accounting provides. Financial accounting cannot compare actual results with budget, and its historical reports are aimed mainly at external users.

questions.question: The shareholders of a Lagos company receive its income statement and statement of financial position for the year just ended. These reports are the product of which branch of accounting?
questions.explanation: Financial accounting produces historical reports, such as the income statement and statement of financial position, for external users like shareholders. Management accounting is the closest wrong choice, but its reports are for managers inside the company, not for shareholders outside it.

questions.question: The keeping and reporting of accounts showing how public funds are received and spent by a federal government ministry is known as
questions.explanation: Public sector accounting, also called government accounting, deals with the accounts of government bodies such as ministries. Taxation is tempting because government collects taxes, but taxation as a branch is about computing and planning tax, not recording how a ministry receives and spends public funds.

questions.question: Public sector accounting is also known as
questions.explanation: Public sector accounting is another name for government accounting, the branch that deals with the accounts of government bodies. Social accounting is a different branch, concerned with the social and environmental effects of an organisation's activities.

questions.question: Apart from the main specialised branches such as auditing and taxation, which of the following is also often listed as a branch of accounting?
questions.explanation: Forensic accounting is often listed among the branches of accounting, along with public sector and social or environmental accounting. Actuarial science, estate management and quantity surveying are separate professions, not branches of accounting.

questions.question: A company in Lagos prepares a report on the effects of its operations on the environment and the local community. This report belongs to which branch of accounting?
questions.explanation: Reporting the effects of a business on society and the environment is social and environmental accounting. Cost accounting may seem related because it deals with costs, but it focuses on product and process costs, not on the firm's impact on the community.

questions.question: Which of these statements correctly describes financial accounting?

options.a: It is an independent examination of accounts
options.b: It is prepared mainly for budget control
options.d: It is mainly concerned with product costs

questions.explanation: Financial accounting records transactions that have already happened, so it is historical in nature. Being prepared mainly for budget control describes management accounting, which serves managers inside the business.

questions.question: A trader in Balogun market keeps his household spending out of his shop's books. Which attribute of financial accounting does this reflect?

options.a: It reports mainly to external users
options.b: It treats the business as a separate entity
options.c: It is concerned with product costs

questions.explanation: Financial accounting treats the business as separate from its owner, so the owner's private spending is not recorded as a business transaction. Being historical is also an attribute of financial accounting, but it explains when transactions are recorded, not why the owner's household spending is kept out.

questions.question: Which of the following best states the main difference between financial accounting and management accounting?

options.a: Financial accounting raises and uses funds; management accounting determines the cost of each product made
options.b: Financial accounting computes tax payable; management accounting examines the financial statements independently
options.c: Financial accounting supports internal planning and control; management accounting gives historical reports to external users
options.d: Financial accounting gives historical reports to external users; management accounting supports internal planning and control

questions.explanation: Financial accounting looks back and reports to outsiders, while management accounting serves managers inside the business with information for planning, control and decisions. The option that swaps the two descriptions is the most tempting trap, because it uses the right ideas but attaches each to the wrong branch.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes financial management from financial accounting?

options.a: Financial management deals with raising and using funds; financial accounting gives historical reports to external users
options.b: Financial management gives historical reports to external users; financial accounting deals with raising and using funds
options.c: Financial management determines product costs; financial accounting supports internal planning and control
options.d: Financial management computes tax payable; financial accounting independently examines the financial statements

questions.explanation: Financial management is about obtaining funds and putting them to use, while financial accounting records past transactions and reports them to outsiders. The option that swaps the two descriptions is the usual trap, since the similar names make the branches easy to mix up.

questions.question: Auditing and financial accounting differ in that

options.a: Auditing independently examines financial statements; financial accounting prepares historical reports for external users
options.b: Auditing prepares historical reports for external users; financial accounting independently examines financial statements
options.c: Auditing determines product and process costs; financial accounting deals with raising and using funds
options.d: Auditing supports internal planning and control; financial accounting computes tax payable

questions.explanation: Financial accounting prepares the financial statements, and auditing is the independent examination of those statements afterwards. The option that reverses the two roles is the most tempting wrong answer, because it uses the correct descriptions but gives each to the wrong branch.

questions.question: Financial accounting does not give the cost of the products a business manufactures. Which branch of accounting fills this gap?
questions.explanation: Cost accounting deals with product and process costs, so it supplies the product costs that financial accounting does not give. Financial management is the most tempting wrong choice, but it is concerned with raising and using funds, not with costing products.

questions.question: Which limitation of financial accounting is usually given as a reason why cost and management accounting are needed?

options.a: It does not give the cost of products manufactured
options.b: It treats the business as a separate entity
options.c: It reports to external users such as lenders
options.d: It is prepared using the double-entry system

questions.explanation: Financial accounting reports on the business as a whole and does not show product costs, budget comparisons or departmental results, which is why cost and management accounting are needed. Treating the business as a separate entity is a basic feature of financial accounting, not a weakness that another branch has to fix.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT usually given as a reason for needing cost and management accounting?

options.a: Financial accounting does not give product costs
options.b: Financial accounting cannot compare results with budget
options.c: Financial accounting does not show departmental results
options.d: Financial accounting treats the business as a separate entity

questions.explanation: Treating the business as separate from its owner is a normal attribute of financial accounting and creates no need for another branch. Missing product costs, no comparison with budget and no departmental results are the gaps usually given as the reason cost and management accounting are needed.

questions.question: The management of a firm in Ikeja wants to know which of its departments are making losses. Which branch of accounting is best placed to provide this information?
questions.explanation: Management accounting gives managers internal information for control and decisions, such as how each department is performing. Financial accounting is the tempting choice, but it reports on the whole business and does not show which departments perform well or make losses.

questions.question: Financial accounting is sometimes likened to a "post-mortem report". This is mainly because it

options.a: Plans how the business will raise funds in future
options.b: Reports on events after they have happened, using historical figures
options.c: Shows the cost of each product the business makes
options.d: Independently examines the accounts for errors and fraud

questions.explanation: Like a post-mortem done after death, financial accounting reports on transactions after they have taken place and relies on historical figures. Independently examining the accounts describes auditing, which is a separate branch rather than the reason for the post-mortem comparison.

questions.question: A firm in Ikeja is deciding whether to replace an old machine and launch a new product. Which branch of accounting is designed to provide information for such decisions?
questions.explanation: Management accounting provides information for internal planning, control and decisions such as replacement, new products and expansion. Financial accounting is the tempting choice, but it does not help with strategic decisions of this kind because it mainly reports historical results.

questions.question: Management accounting information is used for all of the following EXCEPT

options.d: Independent examination of the financial statements

questions.explanation: Independent examination of the financial statements is auditing, not management accounting. Planning, control and decision-making are exactly what management accounting information is used for inside the business.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs correctly matches a branch of accounting with its main concern?

options.b: Cost accounting - product and process costs

questions.explanation: Cost accounting is correctly matched, because it deals with product and process costs. Raising and using funds belongs to financial management, not auditing, while auditing is the independent examination of financial statements.

questions.question: One of these branch-and-concern pairs is mismatched. Which one is it?

options.a: Auditing - independent examination of financial statements
options.b: Financial management - tax computation and planning
options.c: Management accounting - internal planning and control
options.d: Financial accounting - historical reports for external users

questions.explanation: The pairing of financial management with tax computation is wrong, because financial management deals with raising and using funds while tax computation and planning belongs to taxation. The other three pairs, such as auditing with independent examination of financial statements, are all correct.

questions.question: The main users of management accounting information are
questions.explanation: Management accounting is meant for internal planning, control and decisions, so its main users are the business's own managers. Shareholders are users of financial accounting reports, which are historical and prepared mainly for people outside the business.

questions.question: Financial accounting reports are prepared mainly for

options.b: External users such as shareholders and lenders

questions.explanation: Financial accounting produces historical reports for external users such as shareholders and lenders. Preparing reports for managers' budget control describes management accounting, which serves people inside the business.
